stem.value: Which statement best describes what is meant by the term "digital divide"?

content.value: The performance gap between older processor architectures and newer ones
The uneven distribution of access to computing devices, connectivity, and the skills to use them across different populations
The technical difference between representing information as continuous analog signals versus discrete digital values
The separation of a network into subnets so that traffic in one segment does not reach another

explanation.value: The digital divide refers to inequality in who can obtain and effectively use computing technology, driven by factors such as income, geography, age, and education. The choice describing continuous analog signals versus discrete digital values is the analog-to-digital distinction, which sounds related because of the word "digital" but has nothing to do with access inequality.

stem.value: A rural school district issues a laptop to every student, but after a full semester teachers report that homework completion rates have not improved. Which action is most likely to address the underlying obstacle?

content.value: Providing subsidized home broadband service or loaner cellular hotspots to families without internet access
Increasing the amount of memory installed in each student laptop
Replacing the district's learning management system with a competing product
Extending the school computer lab's hours by fifteen minutes each morning

explanation.value: Devices alone do not close the access gap; in rural areas the binding constraint is usually the absence of affordable home connectivity, often called the "homework gap." Extending lab hours helps a few students marginally but does not give the whole population access during the hours when homework is actually done.

stem.value: A teacher is revising a class website so that students who are blind and use screen-reader software can use it. Which change will most directly improve the site for those students?

content.value: Increasing the resolution of all photographs on the page
Raising the contrast ratio between the body text and the page background
Adding meaningful text descriptions to images and marking section titles with real heading elements
Adding background music that plays automatically when the page loads

explanation.value: A screen reader can only announce information that exists as text or structure, so alternative text and true headings give blind users both content and a way to navigate the page. Higher contrast is a genuine accessibility improvement, but it serves users with low vision or color deficiency, not users who are not looking at the screen at all.

stem.value: Which of the following is the principal environmental concern associated with electronic waste from discarded computers and phones?

content.value: Discarded devices continue to draw electrical power after disposal
Toxic substances such as lead, mercury, and cadmium can contaminate soil and groundwater, while valuable recoverable metals are lost
Electronic waste occupies a larger share of landfill volume than any other category of waste
Discarded circuit boards emit radio interference that disrupts nearby wireless networks

explanation.value: E-waste is a small fraction of total waste by volume but a disproportionate share of hazardous material, and it also strands metals like gold and copper that could be recovered. The claim that e-waste occupies a larger share of landfill volume than any other category is a common misconception: e-waste is dangerous because of what it contains, not because of how much space it takes up.

stem.value: A company runs a data center in which most physical servers sit at roughly ten percent utilization. Which change would most reduce the data center's overall energy consumption?

content.value: Consolidating the workloads onto a smaller number of well-utilized servers using virtualization and retiring the surplus machines
Adding additional servers so that the existing load is spread more thinly across the fleet
Scheduling full backups to run overnight instead of during business hours
Replacing the copper network cabling between racks with fiber-optic cabling

explanation.value: An idle server still draws a large fraction of its peak power and still must be cooled, so lightly loaded machines waste energy continuously; consolidation removes that fixed overhead. Spreading load across more servers makes the problem worse, and shifting backup timing moves work around without reducing the total energy used.

stem.value: Which statement most accurately characterizes the effect of automation and computing on employment?

content.value: Automation reduces employment at an equal rate across all occupations and industries
Automation has historically had no measurable effect on the kinds of work people do
The effects are uneven: routine, highly repeatable tasks are the most susceptible to automation, while demand grows for work that automation complements rather than replaces
Only manufacturing work is affected by automation; service and clerical work is not

explanation.value: Automation targets tasks rather than whole occupations, and the tasks most easily automated are routine and rule-governed, which is why the impact falls unevenly across jobs. The claim that only manufacturing work is affected is outdated: clerical work such as data entry, scheduling, and routine customer service has been heavily automated as well.

stem.value: A regional manufacturer automates its assembly line. It plans to hire technicians to maintain and program the new equipment and wants to fill those roles from its current workforce. What is the most significant obstacle to that plan?

content.value: The new equipment will require more floor space than the old line
Displaced assembly workers generally need substantial retraining, which takes time and money that neither they nor the employer may have budgeted
Automated equipment cannot legally be operated by employees who previously did the same work manually
The number of technician positions will exceed the number of assembly positions eliminated

explanation.value: The jobs created by automation typically demand a different and higher skill set than the jobs it eliminates, so the transition is limited by retraining capacity rather than by the existence of openings. The claim that technician positions will outnumber the assembly positions eliminated reverses the usual pattern: automation normally creates fewer maintenance roles than the number of manual roles it displaces.

stem.value: A health system replaces many routine follow-up appointments with video visits. Which is the most realistic drawback of this shift?

content.value: Patients who lack reliable broadband, a suitable device, or the skills to use one may be excluded from care that others now receive more easily
Video technology is unable to transmit images clearly enough for a clinician to see a patient
Video visits necessarily take longer than in-person visits for both patient and clinician
Medical records generated during a video visit cannot be stored electronically

explanation.value: Telehealth improves convenience for people who already have connectivity while potentially widening gaps for rural, low-income, or older patients who do not, which is a classic example of a technology amplifying existing inequality. The other options describe technical limitations that modern video and records systems do not actually have.

stem.value: Which pairing best captures both a benefit and a corresponding drawback of the growth of online retail?

content.value: Shoppers gain wider selection and price comparison, but local brick-and-mortar businesses face competitive pressure and some communities lose nearby stores
Shoppers pay less for goods, but online stores are unable to accept returns
Shoppers can order at any hour, but online catalogs must be smaller than physical store inventories
Shoppers receive items faster, but online retailers cannot sell perishable goods

explanation.value: The best-documented economic effect of e-commerce is a transfer of consumer surplus and market share away from local retail, which affects local employment and, in some areas, physical access to goods. The other options pair a real benefit with a supposed limitation that does not hold in practice.

stem.value: A delivery company finds that several drivers followed turn-by-turn navigation directions onto a road that had been closed for construction for weeks, even though barricades and detour signs were plainly visible. This situation is the clearest example of which concern about computing?

content.value: Insufficient network bandwidth in the delivery vehicles
Over-reliance on automated systems, in which users defer to a system's output instead of exercising independent judgment
A hardware defect in the navigation devices themselves
A user interface whose color scheme is difficult to read in daylight

explanation.value: The system behaved as designed using the data it had; the failure was that drivers trusted stale guidance over direct evidence in front of them, which is automation complacency. Nothing in the scenario indicates a device malfunction, since out-of-date map data is a limitation of the information rather than a hardware fault.

stem.value: A school moves attendance and grade records entirely to a cloud-hosted service, so nothing is stored locally. Which measure best addresses the reliability risk this creates?

content.value: Purchasing a faster internet connection for the main office
Training teachers to use more of the service's optional features
Scheduling regular exports of the data to storage the school controls, along with a documented procedure for operating during an outage
Creating additional administrator accounts within the service

explanation.value: A single external dependency means that a vendor outage, a billing lapse, or a service shutdown can leave the school with no records at all, so the mitigation is an independent copy plus a fallback workflow. A faster connection helps only when the problem is on the school's side, which is the less likely failure here.

stem.value: A district budgets for a one-to-one tablet program by counting only the purchase price of the devices. Which omitted cost is most likely to make the program unsustainable after the first year?

content.value: Sales tax on the initial purchase order
Freight charges for delivering the devices to school sites
Protective cases for the devices
Recurring costs for technical support, repair and replacement, software licensing, network capacity, and teacher training

explanation.value: Total cost of ownership is dominated by ongoing operational expenses that recur every year, not by the one-time acquisition price, and these are the costs that strand technology initiatives once grant funding ends. The other three items are real but small and, unlike support and replacement, they are incurred only once.

stem.value: A community center gives free tablets and free wireless internet to residents of a senior housing complex. Six months later, most of the tablets are rarely used. What is the most appropriate next step?

content.value: Offer ongoing hands-on instruction and a place residents can go for help when they get stuck
Replace the tablets with a newer model that has a faster processor
Increase the bandwidth of the building's internet connection
Distribute a second tablet to each resident

explanation.value: Hardware and connectivity were both already provided, so the remaining barrier is digital literacy and confidence, which is addressed by sustained training and support rather than more equipment. Adding bandwidth or newer devices cannot help people who are not yet comfortable using the devices they have.

stem.value: In many parts of the world, widespread mobile phone use arrived before widespread landline telephone service ever existed. What best explains this pattern?

content.value: Wired telephone equipment does not function reliably in hot or humid climates
Cellular networks require far less fixed infrastructure per subscriber than running copper wire to every building, so coverage can be deployed faster and at lower cost
Most governments in these regions prohibited the construction of wired telephone networks
Mobile handsets were less expensive to manufacture than landline handsets

explanation.value: One cell tower can serve thousands of users across a wide area, whereas wireline service requires physical cable to each individual premises, which is the dominant cost of building out a network. This "leapfrogging" of an infrastructure generation shows that the main obstacle to adoption was the cost of physical build-out rather than demand or regulation.

stem.value: Hospitals that replaced paper charts with electronic health record systems gained searchable, shareable, legible records. Which drawback of that transition has been most widely reported by clinicians?

content.value: Laboratory results can no longer be attached to a patient's record
Substantial time spent on structured data entry during and after patient visits, reducing time available for direct patient care
Records became harder for other clinicians in the same hospital to read
Patient histories can only be retrieved in the order in which they were written

explanation.value: Electronic records shifted documentation burden onto clinicians, who must enter data in the structured form the software requires, and this added workload is a leading contributor to reported burnout. The remaining options describe capabilities that electronic records clearly improved rather than degraded.

stem.value: Accessibility features are often used by far more people than the group they were designed for. Which example best illustrates this principle?

content.value: Captions added for deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers are also used by people watching in noisy places, people learning the language, and people searching video for a spoken phrase
A specialized braille display purchased by a university for a single blind student
A high-resolution monitor bought so that photographs appear sharper
A password manager that stores account credentials for all of an organization's staff

explanation.value: Captions are the standard illustration of the so-called curb-cut effect, in which an accommodation built for one group produces broad secondary benefits for everyone else. The braille display is a genuine assistive technology but one whose usefulness really is confined to the group it targets, which is why it does not illustrate the principle.

stem.value: A student who has limited fine motor control operates a computer entirely from the keyboard and cannot use a mouse. Which design choice in a web application would create the greatest barrier for this student?

content.value: A navigation menu whose submenus appear only while the pointer hovers over them, with no keyboard-reachable equivalent
Body text set in a large, high-contrast typeface
A form in which every input field has a visible, associated label
A page layout that adjusts sensibly when the browser window is resized

explanation.value: Functionality available only through pointer hover is unreachable for anyone navigating by keyboard, which makes those menu items effectively nonexistent for this student. The other three choices are neutral or actively helpful for accessibility.

stem.value: A city uses software to redesign its bus routes, but the ridership counts feeding the software were collected four years ago and no longer reflect where people live and work. Which limitation of computing systems does this best illustrate?

content.value: The algorithm's running time grows too quickly as the number of stops increases
The city needs processors capable of a higher clock speed
The quality of a system's output is bounded by the quality of its input data, and the system itself cannot recognize that its data no longer describes reality
Storage capacity is insufficient to hold four years of ridership records

explanation.value: The program will produce a confident, internally consistent answer to the wrong problem, because nothing in it can detect that the world changed after the data was collected. The other options describe performance or capacity constraints, none of which would be fixed by a faster or larger machine operating on the same stale data.

stem.value: A city has limited funds and wants to help residents who lack home internet access complete online job applications during the coming year. Which approach best fits these constraints?

content.value: Begin construction of a municipal fiber network reaching every residence in the city
Extend public library hours, expand the number of public workstations, and lend mobile hotspots to residents
Mail a printed guide to online job searching to every household
Require local employers to continue accepting paper applications indefinitely

explanation.value: Anchor institutions such as libraries already have connectivity, staff, and equipment, so expanding their capacity delivers access within the stated budget and timeframe. A municipal fiber build might be the better long-term answer, but it takes years and large capital outlays, which the scenario explicitly rules out.

stem.value: An organization wants to reduce the total environmental footprint of the laptops it buys. Which strategy generally has the largest effect?

content.value: Choosing repairable machines with replaceable batteries and keeping each machine in service for more years before replacing it
Buying machines with smaller physical dimensions and lighter weight
Moving employee file storage from local drives to a cloud service
Shortening the replacement cycle so that older, less efficient machines are retired sooner

explanation.value: Most of a laptop's lifetime environmental cost comes from manufacturing rather than from the electricity it uses, so extending service life spreads that fixed cost over more years of use. Shortening the replacement cycle to retire less efficient machines sooner is the tempting trap: replacing devices more often to gain efficiency usually increases the total footprint because it triggers manufacturing more frequently.

stem.value: A county wants to adopt a modern online permitting system, but thirty years of permit records live in a custom mainframe application that no current vendor supports and whose data format is undocumented. Which obstacle to adoption does this scenario primarily illustrate?

content.value: Insufficient broadband capacity at county offices
A lack of basic digital literacy among county staff
The cost and difficulty of migrating from, or integrating with, entrenched legacy systems
Resistance from residents who prefer to submit applications in person

explanation.value: The barrier described is technical debt in existing systems: the historical data must be extracted, understood, and converted before any replacement can go live, and that work often costs more than the new system itself. Nothing in the scenario points to bandwidth, staff skills, or public preference as the blocking factor.

stem.value: A developer writes a program that sorts library records. Under United States copyright law, what does copyright protection cover in this situation?

content.value: The general idea of sorting library records by title
The name the developer chose for the program
The mathematical properties of the sorting algorithm itself
The particular source code the developer wrote to express the sorting program

explanation.value: Copyright protects the fixed, original expression of an idea, which for software means the actual code the author wrote. Ideas, algorithms, and mathematical facts are not copyrightable (they may be eligible for patent protection instead), and short names or titles are handled by trademark law rather than copyright.

stem.value: A company builds a commercial inventory application and links it with a library released under a strong copyleft license such as the GNU General Public License. If the company distributes the finished application to customers, what does the copyleft license most directly require?

content.value: The company must give the application away at no charge.
The company must transfer ownership of its code to the library's original author.
The company must make the corresponding source code of the distributed work available under the same license terms.
The company must obtain written permission from the library's author before each release.

explanation.value: Copyleft licenses permit reuse but require that derivative works, when distributed, carry the same license and make source code available. Charging money is still allowed, which is why the 'must be free of charge' option is the common misconception; copyleft restricts licensing terms, not price, and it never transfers ownership.

stem.value: An engineering team invents a novel, non-obvious method for compressing sensor data and wants legal protection for the method itself, not merely for one implementation of it. Which form of intellectual property protection is the appropriate fit?

content.value: A utility patent
A copyright registration
A trademark registration
A creative commons license

explanation.value: A patent can protect a novel, useful, and non-obvious process or method, which is exactly what the team wants to cover. Copyright would protect only the specific code written to implement the method, a trademark protects brand identifiers, and a Creative Commons license is a way to grant permissions in work you already own, not a form of protection.

stem.value: A software firm keeps the internal design of its recommendation engine confidential, requires employees to sign nondisclosure agreements, and never publishes the design. This approach relies on which category of intellectual property protection?

content.value: Public domain dedication
Patent
Trademark
Trade secret

explanation.value: Trade secret protection comes from keeping commercially valuable information secret and taking reasonable measures such as nondisclosure agreements to preserve that secrecy. A patent would require publicly disclosing the design in exchange for a time-limited monopoly, which is the opposite of what the firm is doing.

stem.value: When courts evaluate whether a use of copyrighted material qualifies as fair use, which of the following is one of the recognized statutory factors?

content.value: Whether the person who copied the work gave credit to the author
Whether the copied material was obtained from a website rather than from print
The effect of the use upon the potential market for or value of the copyrighted work
Whether the copyright holder was notified in advance of the copying

explanation.value: Market effect is one of the four statutory fair use factors, along with purpose and character of the use, nature of the work, and amount used. Giving credit is good academic practice but does not by itself make a use fair, and neither the medium of the source nor advance notice is part of the legal analysis.

stem.value: A student completing an individual programming assignment finds a helpful function in a public online forum, pastes it into the submission, and changes only the variable names. The assignment instructions permit consulting outside sources but require that any borrowed code be identified. What is the most accurate assessment of the student's action?

content.value: It is acceptable because renaming the variables makes the code the student's own work.
It is plagiarism because the student presented another author's work as original without the required attribution.
It is acceptable because code posted publicly online carries no authorship claims.
It is a copyright violation but not an academic integrity issue.

explanation.value: Plagiarism is presenting someone else's work as your own, and superficial edits such as renaming identifiers do not change authorship. Publicly posted code still has an author and usually a license, and the assignment explicitly required attribution, so the failure is an academic integrity violation regardless of any separate copyright question.

stem.value: A school purchases one single-seat license of a proprietary graphics program and installs it on twenty lab computers so an entire class can use it at once. Which statement best describes this situation?

content.value: It is permitted because the school bought the software and may install it on hardware it owns.
It is permitted because the use is educational rather than commercial.
It violates the license agreement, which grants a limited right to use the software on a specified number of machines.
It is permitted as long as only one student uses the program at any given moment.

explanation.value: Buying proprietary software purchases a license to use it under stated terms, not ownership of the software itself, and a single-seat license limits the number of installations. Educational use does not automatically override license terms, and the vendor, not the customer, defines whether a concurrent-use model is available.

stem.value: How does a permissive open-source license, such as the MIT license, most significantly differ from a copyleft open-source license?

content.value: A permissive license allows the code to be incorporated into closed-source products, while copyleft requires derivative works to remain openly licensed.
A permissive license places the code in the public domain, while copyleft retains the author's copyright.
A permissive license forbids commercial use, while copyleft allows it.
A permissive license expires after a fixed term, while copyleft lasts indefinitely.

explanation.value: Both license families are open source and both keep the author's copyright, but permissive licenses impose few conditions beyond preserving the notice, so the code may be folded into proprietary products. Copyleft adds the reciprocity requirement that distributed derivative works stay under the same open terms.

stem.value: Which statement correctly describes a work that is in the public domain?

content.value: It is any work that has been posted on a publicly accessible website.
It may be used only for noncommercial purposes.
It may be used only if the user pays a royalty to a central licensing body.
It may be used freely by anyone because no copyright restrictions apply to it.

explanation.value: A public domain work is one whose copyright has expired, was forfeited, or was deliberately relinquished, so anyone may copy, modify, or sell it without permission. Merely posting a work publicly online does not place it in the public domain, which is the most common misunderstanding here.

stem.value: A hospital deploys a machine learning model that predicts which patients need follow-up care. Reviewers discover the model recommends follow-up far less often for one demographic group, even for patients with similar medical needs. Which explanation most commonly accounts for this kind of outcome?

content.value: The historical data used to train the model reflected existing disparities in care, which the model learned and reproduced.
Machine learning models produce random output when given large data sets.
The programmers must have deliberately inserted a rule that excludes the group.
Computers cannot process categorical variables, so the results are meaningless.

explanation.value: Algorithmic bias most often arises when training data encodes past inequities or is unrepresentative, and the model then reproduces those patterns at scale. Intentional discriminatory code is possible but rare compared with data-driven bias, and the remaining options misstate how models behave.

stem.value: Shortly before release, a software engineer discovers a defect that could cause a medical device to report incorrect dosage readings. A manager asks the engineer to stay quiet so the launch date is not missed. According to widely adopted professional codes of ethics for computing practitioners, what should the engineer do?

content.value: Follow the manager's instruction, since responsibility for the decision rests with management.
Report the defect through appropriate channels, because avoiding harm to the public takes precedence over schedule pressure.
Post details of the defect on a public forum immediately to force a fix.
Quietly remove the affected feature without telling anyone, so the schedule holds.

explanation.value: Professional codes of conduct place public safety and avoiding harm above employer convenience, and they direct practitioners to disclose risks through appropriate internal and, if necessary, external channels. Immediate public disclosure skips the required escalation steps, and silently altering the product conceals rather than addresses the risk.

stem.value: A course syllabus states that generative AI tools may be used to brainstorm approaches but that any AI-produced code must be disclosed in a comment. A student uses an AI assistant to write an entire submitted program and adds no disclosure. Which principle does this most directly violate?

content.value: Copyright law, because AI-generated text is always owned by the tool's vendor
Data privacy, because the student's prompt was transmitted to a server
Academic integrity, because the student misrepresented the origin of the submitted work
Fair use, because the student did not license the generated code

explanation.value: The stated policy allowed AI use with disclosure, so the violation is the misrepresentation of authorship rather than the use of the tool itself. Ownership of AI output and the privacy of prompts are separate questions that do not describe what the student did wrong here.

stem.value: A fitness app collects users' step counts, telling them at sign-up that the data is used to display personal activity charts. A year later the company wants to sell aggregated movement patterns to advertisers. What is the ethically appropriate step before doing so?

content.value: Proceed, because the company owns the servers on which the data is stored.
Inform users of the new purpose and obtain their consent for it.
Proceed, because aggregated data can never be traced to individuals.
Proceed after deleting user names from the database, with no further notice.

explanation.value: Purpose limitation holds that data collected for one stated reason should not be repurposed without notifying users and obtaining consent for the new use. Owning the infrastructure confers no ethical right to the data, and aggregation or name removal reduces but does not eliminate re-identification risk, so neither substitutes for consent.

stem.value: A website offers two designs for its location-sharing feature. In design 1, location sharing is off until the user turns it on. In design 2, location sharing is on by default and the user must find a setting to turn it off. Which statement about these designs is accurate?

content.value: Design 1 is an opt-in model and is generally considered the stronger protection of user privacy.
Design 2 is an opt-in model and is generally considered the stronger protection of user privacy.
The two designs are ethically equivalent because the same setting is available in both.
Design 1 is an opt-out model that shifts the burden of protection onto the user.

explanation.value: Opt-in means the user must take an affirmative action before data is collected, which is design 1 and is the privacy-protective default. Design 2 is opt-out; although the same control exists, defaults strongly shape behavior, so the two designs are not ethically equivalent.

stem.value: While designing a new school lunch-ordering system, a team decides to store only a student identifier and the menu selection, rather than the home address, birth date, and phone number that the database could hold. This decision best illustrates which privacy principle?

content.value: Data minimization
Redundancy
Load balancing
Non-repudiation

explanation.value: Data minimization, a core element of privacy by design, means collecting and retaining only the data actually required for the system's purpose, which shrinks the harm if a breach occurs. The other terms describe reliability, performance, and authentication concepts rather than limits on data collection.

stem.value: Which of the following stored fields would most clearly be classified as personally identifiable information?

content.value: The total number of accounts created on a site in a given month
The version number of the server software
The average session length across all site visitors
A user's Social Security number

explanation.value: Personally identifiable information is data that can identify a specific individual either alone or combined with other data, and a Social Security number identifies one person directly. Aggregate counts and averages describe a population rather than an individual, and software version numbers describe the system.

stem.value: A teacher wants to post an online leaderboard showing each student's full name next to that student's course grades so the class can compare progress. In the United States, which consideration most directly governs this plan?

content.value: Federal law protecting the privacy of student education records restricts disclosure of individually identifiable grade information without consent.
Copyright law, because the grades are original works authored by the teacher.
Patent law, because the leaderboard is a new method of displaying data.
No legal consideration applies, because grades are generated by the school rather than by the students.

explanation.value: Student education records, including individually identifiable grades, are protected from disclosure without appropriate consent, so publishing named grades to the class is not permissible. Copyright and patent law address authorship and inventions, neither of which governs the disclosure of a student's personal record.

stem.value: An online retailer discovers that attackers copied a customer database containing names, email addresses, and stored payment details. Which consequence for the affected individuals is the most direct result of this breach?

content.value: Their personal computers will run more slowly.
Their internet service will be interrupted.
They face elevated risk of identity theft and fraudulent charges made in their names.
Their previously placed orders will be automatically cancelled.

explanation.value: A breach of identifying and financial data exposes individuals to identity theft, fraudulent transactions, and targeted follow-on scams that use the stolen details to appear credible. The other options describe effects on the victims' own devices or service, which a server-side data breach does not cause.

stem.value: A research group publishes a data set it describes as anonymous because names and account numbers were removed, but each record still lists a birth date, ZIP code, and gender. Why is the group's privacy claim questionable?

content.value: Removing a name always leaves the file corrupted and unusable.
The combination of remaining attributes can be cross-referenced with other data sources to re-identify individuals.
Anonymous data sets may not legally be published in any form.
Birth dates and ZIP codes are copyrighted by the agencies that issue them.

explanation.value: Quasi-identifiers such as birth date, ZIP code, and gender are individually common but in combination can be nearly unique, allowing linkage against voter rolls or other public records to re-identify people. True anonymization therefore requires treating these attribute combinations, not merely deleting explicit identifiers.

stem.value: A user visits a news site and notices that advertisements for a product viewed on an unrelated shopping site now appear there. Which mechanism most likely explains this?

content.value: Third-party tracking cookies or similar identifiers shared across sites by the same advertising network
The news site reading files stored elsewhere on the user's hard drive
The user's operating system broadcasting purchase history to all open applications
A coincidence, since browsers make it technically impossible to correlate activity across sites

explanation.value: Cross-site advertising works because the same ad network is embedded in many sites and can recognize a returning browser through third-party cookies or equivalent identifiers, building a profile of browsing behavior. Browsers sandbox pages from the local file system, so the other explanations are not how this tracking occurs.

stem.value: An employee receives an urgent email that appears to come from the payroll department, warns that direct deposit will be suspended today, and links to a page asking for the employee's login credentials. Which characterization and response are most appropriate?

content.value: It is safe if the sender's display name matches a real department, since display names cannot be forged.
It is a routine notice; the employee should enter the credentials quickly to avoid losing pay.
It is a denial-of-service attack; the employee should restart the computer.
It is likely a phishing attempt; the employee should not use the link and should verify the request through a known official channel.

explanation.value: Manufactured urgency plus a link requesting credentials is the signature pattern of phishing, and the correct response is to avoid the embedded link and confirm through an independently known contact or address. Sender display names are trivially spoofed, so a familiar-looking name is not evidence of legitimacy.

stem.value: A caller telephones a school office, claims to be a technician from the district help desk, says a server migration is failing, and asks the secretary to read back the office account password so the work can continue. This scenario is best described as an example of

content.value: social engineering, in which an attacker manipulates a person rather than defeating a technical control.
a brute-force attack, in which many password guesses are tried in sequence.
a software vulnerability being exploited in the telephone system.
a legitimate maintenance procedure, since help desk staff routinely need user passwords.

explanation.value: Social engineering exploits human trust and authority cues to obtain information that technical safeguards would otherwise protect, which is exactly what the pretext call attempts. Legitimate support staff can reset or access accounts through administrative tools and do not need a user to disclose a password.

stem.value: Two users each protect several online accounts. User 1 chooses one long, complex password and reuses it everywhere. User 2 chooses a different long password for each account and enables multi-factor authentication. Which statement best compares the two approaches?

content.value: User 1 is better protected, because a single complex password is harder to guess than several.
User 2 is better protected, because a breach at one site does not unlock the other accounts and a stolen password alone is insufficient to log in.
The approaches are equivalent, because password complexity is the only factor that matters.
User 2 is worse protected, because multi-factor authentication stores the password in more places.

explanation.value: Reused passwords enable credential stuffing: once one site is breached, attackers replay the same credentials elsewhere, so complexity does not help. Unique passwords contain the damage to a single account, and a second authentication factor means a stolen password by itself is not enough to gain access.

stem.value: A user opens an email attachment, and shortly afterward the files on the computer become unreadable and a message demands payment in exchange for restoring access. Which category of malware does this describe?

content.value: Adware
A rootkit
A keylogger
Ransomware

explanation.value: Ransomware encrypts or otherwise locks a victim's data and demands payment for restoration, which matches the described behavior exactly. A keylogger silently records keystrokes, adware displays unwanted advertising, and a rootkit conceals an intruder's ongoing access, so none of them extort the user directly.

stem.value: What is the decimal value of the unsigned binary numeral 1011010?

explanation.value: Reading the place values from the left, the digits sit in the 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, and 1 columns. The 1 digits occupy the 64, 16, 8, and 2 columns, so the total is 64 + 16 + 8 + 2 = 90. Answers such as 82 come from dropping or misplacing one of the middle place values.

stem.value: Which binary numeral is equivalent to the decimal number 45?

explanation.value: Subtracting the largest fitting powers of two gives 45 = 32 + 8 + 4 + 1, which lights up the 32, 8, 4, and 1 columns and yields 101101. The tempting distractor 101011 is the same digits in a different order and equals 32 + 8 + 2 + 1 = 43.

stem.value: What is the decimal value of the hexadecimal numeral 2F?

explanation.value: In base 16 the left digit counts sixteens and the right digit counts ones, so 2F is (2 x 16) + 15 = 32 + 15 = 47. The distractor 31 comes from treating F as 15 but the leading 2 as merely 16, and 62 comes from doubling 31.

stem.value: Which hexadecimal numeral represents the decimal number 200?

content.value: B8
C8
D0

explanation.value: Dividing 200 by 16 gives 12 with a remainder of 8, and 12 is written as C in hexadecimal, so the answer is C8. B8 would be (11 x 16) + 8 = 184, and D0 would be 13 x 16 = 208.

stem.value: Which hexadecimal numeral is equivalent to the binary numeral 11010110?

content.value: C6
D6
DA
6D

explanation.value: Group the bits into nibbles of four starting from the right: 1101 and 0110. The first group is 13, written D, and the second group is 6, giving D6. The distractor 6D is the two nibbles converted correctly but written in reversed order.

stem.value: Which binary numeral is equivalent to the hexadecimal numeral 1A3?

explanation.value: Each hexadecimal digit expands to exactly four bits: 1 becomes 0001, A becomes 1010, and 3 becomes 0011, giving 0001 1010 0011. Dropping the leading zeros leaves 110100011. The distractors mistranslate A, which is 10 and therefore 1010, not 1110 or 1101.

stem.value: What is the sum of the unsigned binary numerals 1011 and 1101, expressed in binary?

explanation.value: The two values are 11 and 13 in decimal, and 11 + 13 = 24, which is 16 + 8 and therefore 11000 in binary. The most common error is losing one of the carries that ripple leftward through the three rightmost columns, which produces a result that is too small.

stem.value: A field in a data format stores an unsigned integer using exactly 6 bits. Which of the following decimal values CANNOT be stored in that field?

explanation.value: Six bits produce 2^6 = 64 distinct patterns, which represent the unsigned values 0 through 63. The value 64 requires a seventh bit, so it cannot be stored. The value 63 is representable precisely because it is the all-ones pattern 111111.

stem.value: How many distinct values can be represented by a sequence of 10 bits?

explanation.value: Each additional bit doubles the number of possible patterns, so n bits give 2^n combinations and 10 bits give 2^10 = 1,024. The distractor 1,000 is the frequently used approximation for 2^10, but the exact count is 1,024.

stem.value: What is the result of adding the hexadecimal numerals 3C and 25, expressed in hexadecimal?

content.value: 5F

explanation.value: Converting to decimal, 3C is 60 and 25 is 37, so the sum is 97, and 97 = (6 x 16) + 1 = 61 in hexadecimal. Working directly in base 16, C + 5 is 17 decimal, which is 1 with a carry of 1, and 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. The distractor 51 results from forgetting to propagate that carry into the sixteens column.

stem.value: Programmers often write long bit patterns in hexadecimal rather than binary. What property of hexadecimal makes it a convenient shorthand for binary?

content.value: Each hexadecimal digit corresponds to exactly four binary digits.
Hexadecimal can represent values that binary cannot represent.
Hexadecimal numerals are stored in memory using fewer bits than binary numerals.
Hexadecimal uses only the digits 0 through 9, which people already read fluently.

explanation.value: Because 16 = 2^4, every hexadecimal digit maps onto one group of four bits with no ambiguity, so conversion is a simple digit-by-digit substitution in either direction. The claim that hexadecimal numerals occupy fewer bits in memory is a common misconception: the base is only a notation for humans, and the value occupies the same bits no matter how it is written.

stem.value: A Web page specifies a color as #00FF7F, where the three pairs of hexadecimal digits give the red, green, and blue components in that order. What are the red, green, and blue values in decimal?

red 0, green 255, blue 79
red 0, green 165, blue 127
red 255, green 127, blue 0

stem.value: An image format stores each pixel using 8 bits for red, 8 bits for green, and 8 bits for blue. Approximately how many distinct colors can a single pixel represent?

explanation.value: Each 8-bit channel has 256 levels, and the channels are chosen independently, so the counts multiply: 256 x 256 x 256 = 2^24 = 16,777,216. The distractor 768 comes from adding the three channel counts instead of multiplying them.

stem.value: In a character encoding, the uppercase letter A has the code value 65 and the remaining uppercase letters follow in alphabetical order with consecutive code values. What is the binary representation of the code value for the letter F?

explanation.value: F is the sixth letter, so its code is 65 + 5 = 70, and 70 = 64 + 4 + 2, which is 1000110 in binary. The tempting distractor 1000101 is 69 -- E's code, not F's -- which comes from counting F as 4 letters after A instead of 5, an off-by-one error that fails to count A itself as the first letter.

stem.value: A school needs to assign a unique binary code to each of 300 students. What is the smallest number of bits that can give every student a distinct code?

explanation.value: The requirement is the smallest n for which 2^n is at least 300. Since 2^8 = 256 is too few and 2^9 = 512 is enough, 9 bits are needed. The answer 300 confuses the number of items with the number of bits, which would be the count for a one-bit-per-student scheme rather than a compact binary code.

stem.value: Which statement best describes abstraction as it is used in computing?

content.value: Suppressing details that are not relevant at a given level so that the essential behavior can be used and reasoned about
Rewriting a program so that it uses fewer lines of source code
Translating a program from a high-level language into machine code
Testing a program with a wide range of representative inputs

explanation.value: Abstraction manages complexity by exposing what something does while hiding how it does it, letting a programmer work at one level without holding the lower levels in mind. Reducing the number of lines of source code describes code golf or refactoring for brevity, which may or may not involve abstraction and is not what the term means.

content.value: The student can use the procedure correctly by knowing its name, inputs, and output, without knowing how it computes the result.
The procedure will run faster than the same calculation written directly in the student's own code.
The procedure guarantees that the student's variable trip cannot be assigned an incorrect value.
The procedure removes the need for the student's program to store any data in memory.

explanation.value: A procedure header acts as a contract: it names the operation and describes what goes in and what comes out, which is all a caller needs. The implementation can be replaced with a different formula or algorithm without breaking the calling code. The answer about running faster confuses abstraction with optimization; hiding the body says nothing about its speed.

stem.value: Which statement best describes decomposition in computational thinking?

content.value: Breaking a large problem into smaller subproblems that can be solved and verified more easily
Identifying similarities among problems so that one solution can serve several of them
Removing unnecessary details so that only the essential features of a problem remain
Writing a precise, ordered sequence of steps that always terminates

explanation.value: Decomposition is specifically the act of splitting one large problem into smaller parts that can be tackled separately. Identifying similarities across problems describes pattern recognition, removing inessential detail describes abstraction, and writing a precise ordered sequence of steps describes algorithm design, all of which are related computational-thinking practices but are not decomposition.

stem.value: A student is building a program that manages a library's book catalog. Which action is the clearest example of decomposition?

content.value: Planning separate modules for adding a book, checking a book out, and generating an overdue report, and defining how they exchange data
Choosing shorter variable names so that each line of the program fits on the screen
Converting the catalog's identification numbers from decimal to hexadecimal
Running the finished program on a large sample catalog to measure how long it takes

explanation.value: Splitting the system into independently designed and testable modules with defined interfaces is decomposition in its standard form. The other options are cosmetic formatting, a data-representation change, and performance testing, none of which divide the problem into subproblems.

stem.value: Which statement best describes pattern recognition as a computational-thinking practice?

content.value: Noticing that several problems or subproblems share a common structure so that one general solution can be applied to all of them
Searching a body of text for a specific sequence of characters
Arranging a program's statements so that similar statements are grouped visually
Choosing the data type that uses the fewest bits for each variable in a program

explanation.value: Pattern recognition means spotting shared structure and generalizing, which is what makes reusable procedures, loops, and library functions possible. Searching text for a sequence of characters is an unrelated programming task that happens to use the word pattern in a different technical sense.

stem.value: A programming language lets a developer define a Student type that bundles a name, an identification number, and a list of grades into one value. This feature is best described as which kind of abstraction?

content.value: Data abstraction, because related values are treated as a single unit with a meaningful name
Procedural abstraction, because a sequence of steps is given a name and reused
Hardware abstraction, because memory addresses are chosen automatically
No abstraction, because the individual fields are still visible to the programmer

stem.value: In a high-level language, a programmer writes counter <- counter + 1 rather than manipulating a specific memory location. Which statement best explains the role of the variable name in this example?

content.value: The name is an abstraction for a storage location, so the programmer need not track the actual address where the value is kept.
The name causes the value to be stored in the processor rather than in memory, which makes the program correct.
The name prevents the stored value from being changed by any other part of the program.
The name determines how many bits the value will occupy, independently of its data type.

explanation.value: A variable name is a human-meaningful stand-in for a machine-level storage location, and the language and its translator handle the mapping. The answer about the name determining the number of bits reverses the relationship: storage size is governed by the declared data type, not by the identifier the programmer chooses.

stem.value: Which of the following represents the GREATEST value?

content.value: The binary numeral 110001
The hexadecimal numeral 30
The decimal numeral 47
The binary numeral 101110

stem.value: A binary numeral has a single 0 appended to its right end, so 1011 becomes 10110. What is the effect on the value represented?

The value increases by 1.
The value is multiplied by 2.

stem.value: A team decomposes a payroll system into modules. Which pair of modules is decomposed in the way most likely to make the system easy to change later?

content.value: A tax-calculation module and a paycheck-printing module, each usable through a small set of defined inputs and outputs
A first-half-of-the-code module and a second-half-of-the-code module, split at the midpoint of the source file
A module for lines written by one teammate and a module for lines written by another teammate
A module holding every variable in the system and a module holding every statement in the system

The other options split by file position, authorship, or syntax category, which cuts across responsibilities and leaves the parts tangled together.

stem.value: In an 8-bit two's complement representation, what value does the bit pattern 11111111 represent?

explanation.value: In two's complement, adding 1 to the all-ones pattern carries out of the top bit and leaves 00000000, so the all-ones pattern must be -1. The distractor 255 is the value of the same bits read as an unsigned integer, which shows that a bit pattern has no meaning until an interpretation is chosen.

stem.value: What is the range of integers that can be represented in 8-bit two's complement form?

content.value: 0 through 255
-127 through 127

explanation.value: Eight bits give 256 patterns, and two's complement devotes half of them to negatives, one to zero, and the rest to positives, producing -128 through 127. The asymmetry arises because zero occupies one of the non-negative patterns, so there is one more negative value than positive value.

stem.value: A standard library provides a procedure that returns a list of values arranged in increasing order. Which detail is appropriately hidden from a programmer who calls this procedure?

content.value: The particular step-by-step method the library uses internally to arrange the values
The type of value the procedure returns
The number and order of the arguments the procedure requires
Whether the procedure modifies the caller's original list

explanation.value: Abstraction hides the implementation while the interface stays visible, so the internal method may change between library versions without affecting callers. The other three items are part of the contract the caller must rely on; hiding whether the original list is modified, in particular, would make the procedure impossible to use safely.

stem.value: Two students decompose a weather-dashboard project so they can work at the same time. Which additional step is MOST important for making their separate work fit together?

content.value: Agreeing in advance on the exact inputs and outputs each part will provide to the other
Agreeing to write the same number of lines of code each
Agreeing to use the same text editor and color theme
Agreeing to finish both parts on the same day

explanation.value: Decomposition only pays off when the boundaries between parts are defined, because the interface is the contract that lets each piece be built and tested without waiting on the other. Equal line counts, shared tooling, and matching deadlines are conveniences that do nothing to guarantee the parts will connect.

stem.value: A student has already written a program that reports the total rainfall for each month from a list of daily rainfall readings. She is now asked to report the total sales for each week from a list of daily sales figures. Recognizing that the second task has the same structure as the first is an example of which practice?

content.value: Pattern recognition
Debugging
Data validation
Version control

explanation.value: Both tasks reduce to grouping a sequence of daily numbers into fixed periods and summing each group, so noticing that shared shape and reusing the earlier solution is pattern recognition. Debugging, validation, and version control are all real practices but none of them describe generalizing across two similar problems.

stem.value: What is the product of the unsigned binary numerals 1011 and 100, expressed in binary?

explanation.value: Binary 100 is decimal 4, and multiplying by 4 shifts the other numeral two places to the left, turning 1011 into 101100. Checking in decimal, 11 x 4 = 44 = 32 + 8 + 4 = 101100. The distractor 1011000 is a shift of three places, which would multiply by 8 instead of 4.

stem.value: A team replaces the internal code of a procedure with a completely different method that produces the same results for the same inputs. Programs that call the procedure continue to work without being edited. This outcome is possible primarily because of which principle?

content.value: The procedure's interface is separate from its implementation.
Every high-level language is eventually translated into machine code.
Any two procedures that return the same data type may be substituted for each other.
Procedures are stored in memory separately from the data they operate on.

explanation.value: Callers depend only on the published interface, so any implementation that honors it can be swapped in, which is the practical payoff of procedural abstraction. The claim that any two procedures with the same return type are interchangeable is a tempting overgeneralization: matching return types is not enough, because the substituted procedure must also produce the same results for the same inputs.

stem.value: An uncompressed grayscale image is 100 pixels wide and 100 pixels tall, and each pixel is stored using 8 bits. How many bytes of storage does the image data require?

explanation.value: The image holds 100 x 100 = 10,000 pixels, and at 8 bits each that is 80,000 bits, which is 80,000 / 8 = 10,000 bytes. The distractor 80,000 is the count in bits rather than bytes, and 1,250 comes from dividing the pixel count by 8 instead of multiplying by one byte per pixel.

stem.value: A single statement in a high-level language adds a price to a running total and stores the result. Which statement best describes the relationship between that one statement and what the processor actually does?

content.value: The one statement typically corresponds to several lower-level machine operations, such as loading values, performing the addition, and storing the result.
The one statement always corresponds to exactly one machine operation, which is why high-level languages are faster.
The processor executes the high-level statement directly, without any translation.
The one statement corresponds to no machine operations, because addition is handled by the operating system.

explanation.value: A high-level statement is an abstraction over a group of machine-level steps, and the translator expands it into the loads, arithmetic, and stores the hardware requires. The one-machine-operation answer is the common misconception that the apparent one-to-one look of source lines carries down to the machine level; in fact the compression of many machine steps into one readable statement is exactly the benefit the abstraction provides.

stem.value: A procedure examines every possible pair of distinct items drawn from a list of n items, doing a fixed, constant amount of work for each pair. Which growth rate best describes the total work as n gets large?

content.value: Constant
Logarithmic
Linear
Quadratic

explanation.value: The number of distinct pairs from n items is n * (n - 1) / 2. Multiplying out gives a term in n squared, so the work grows quadratically: tripling n multiplies the work by roughly 9. Linear is the tempting wrong choice because there is only one list being processed, but each item is paired with every other item, which means the list is effectively swept once per item.

stem.value: Which condition must hold before a binary search can correctly be used to locate a value in an array?

content.value: The array must contain no duplicate values.
The array elements must already be arranged in sorted order.
The number of elements in the array must be a power of 2.
The value being searched for must actually be present in the array.

explanation.value: Binary search works by comparing the target to a middle element and then discarding the half that cannot contain the target. That decision is only valid if the elements are in sorted order. Duplicates are permitted (the search simply may find any one of them), the length may be any positive number, and a binary search on a value that is absent correctly reports failure rather than breaking.

stem.value: A linear search is run on an array of 40 elements, looking for a value that is not in the array at all. How many array elements does the search compare to the target before it can report failure?

explanation.value: A linear search cannot conclude that a value is absent until it has ruled out every element, so all 40 are compared. The answer 20 is tempting because the average number of comparisons for a successful search is about half the array, but that average applies only when the target is present; an unsuccessful search always costs the full n. The answer 6 would be the cost of a binary search, which is not applicable here.

stem.value: A binary search is performed on a sorted array of 1,000 elements. In the worst case, approximately how many elements are examined before the search finishes?

explanation.value: Each examination cuts the remaining range roughly in half, so the worst case is about the number of times 1,000 can be halved before reaching a single element. Since 2 to the 10th power is 1,024, that is about 10 examinations. The answer 500 reflects a linear search's average cost, and 32 is the square root of 1,000, which is not the growth rate of binary search.

stem.value: A selection sort arranges an array into increasing order by repeatedly finding the smallest remaining value and placing it at the front of the unsorted portion. After the first three passes have completed on an array of 10 elements, what is guaranteed to be true?

content.value: The three smallest values in the array occupy positions 0, 1, and 2, in increasing order.
The three largest values in the array occupy the last three positions, in increasing order.
The first three positions hold the values that were originally there, but in increasing order.
Exactly three adjacent pairs of elements have been swapped into the correct relative order.

explanation.value: Each pass of a selection sort scans the entire unsorted region, finds the minimum, and moves it to the boundary. After k passes the k smallest values in the whole array are in the first k positions in order, and they never move again. The claim that the first three positions hold the values that were originally there, merely reordered, is wrong because the values placed there come from anywhere in the array, not just the first three positions. The choice that puts the three largest values at the end describes a variant that selects maximums from the back, which is not what was described.

stem.value: A bubble sort makes one complete pass over the array {5, 1, 4, 2, 8}, comparing each adjacent pair from left to right and swapping the two values whenever the left one is larger. What does the array contain when that single pass finishes?

explanation.value: Trace the four adjacent comparisons. Compare 5 and 1: swap, giving {1, 5, 4, 2, 8}. Compare 5 and 4: swap, giving {1, 4, 5, 2, 8}. Compare 5 and 2: swap, giving {1, 4, 2, 5, 8}. Compare 5 and 8: no swap. The result is {1, 4, 2, 5, 8}. The fully sorted array {1, 2, 4, 5, 8} takes more than one pass; a single bubble pass only guarantees that the largest value has reached the end.

stem.value: An insertion sort processes the array {7, 3, 9, 2} from left to right, taking each element in turn and inserting it into its correct place among the already-processed elements to its left. What does the array contain immediately after the element originally at index 2 has been inserted?

explanation.value: Insertion sort begins with index 1. The value 3 is compared to 7, is smaller, and shifts left, giving {3, 7, 9, 2}. Next the value 9 at index 2 is compared to 7, is larger, and therefore stays where it is, leaving {3, 7, 9, 2}. The 2 at index 3 has not been processed yet, so the array is not yet fully sorted; the fully sorted {2, 3, 7, 9} is the final result after all elements are inserted, not the state at this point.

stem.value: Which description best captures how a merge sort orders a list?

content.value: It repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them until no swaps are needed.
It splits the list into halves, sorts each half by the same method, and then combines the two sorted halves into one ordered list.
It scans the unsorted region for the smallest value and moves it to the front, repeating until nothing is unsorted.
It jumps to the middle of the list and discards whichever half cannot contain the next value it needs.

explanation.value: Merge sort is a divide-and-conquer method: divide the list in half, sort each half the same way, then merge the two sorted halves by repeatedly taking whichever front element is smaller. Repeatedly comparing and swapping adjacent elements describes bubble sort, and scanning the unsorted region for the smallest value and moving it to the front describes selection sort. Jumping to the middle of the list and discarding the half that cannot contain the needed value describes binary search, which is a searching method, not a sorting method.

stem.value: The merge step of a merge sort is combining the two sorted lists {2, 5, 8} and {1, 3, 9} into a single sorted list. Working from the front of each list, what are the first four values placed into the combined list, in order?

explanation.value: The merge compares the two front values and takes the smaller each time. Compare 2 and 1: take 1. Compare 2 and 3: take 2. Compare 5 and 3: take 3. Compare 5 and 9: take 5. The first four values are 1, 2, 3, 5. The sequence 2, 1, 5, 3 is the tempting wrong answer because it alternates between the lists, but a merge does not alternate; it always takes the smaller of the two current front values.

stem.value: An algorithm reduces the size of the data it still has to consider by exactly half at every step. Starting from 64 items, how many steps does it take to reduce the amount under consideration to a single item?

explanation.value: The sequence is 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, which is six halvings. This is the defining behavior of logarithmic growth: 2 to the 6th power is 64. The answer 8 is the square root of 64 and 32 is half of it, neither of which measures repeated halving.

stem.value: A program receives an unsorted array of 1,000,000 readings and must determine, one single time, whether a particular reading appears in it. The array will not be used again afterward. Which approach is most efficient?

content.value: Sort the array first, then use binary search, because binary search is faster than linear search.
Use a linear search directly on the unsorted array.
Sort the array first, then use a linear search, because linear search is more reliable on sorted data.
Compare every element to every other element to build an ordering, then search.

explanation.value: A single linear search costs about n steps. Sorting first costs at least on the order of n log n, which is more than n, and that cost is paid before the faster binary search even begins. Since the array is searched only once and then discarded, the sorting cost can never be recovered. Sorting first and then using binary search is the tempting answer because binary search really is faster per search, but the setup cost dominates when there is only one search.

stem.value: Which of the following operations on an array of n elements takes a constant amount of time regardless of how large n is?

content.value: Retrieving the element stored at a given index.
Finding the smallest element in an unsorted array.
Counting how many elements are greater than zero.
Rearranging the elements into increasing order.

explanation.value: An array index maps directly to a memory location, so reading a[i] takes the same time whether the array holds 10 elements or 10 million. Finding the smallest element in an unsorted array and counting how many elements are greater than zero both require inspecting every element, which is linear, and rearranging the elements into increasing order is a sort, which is worse than linear. Constant time means the cost does not depend on n at all, not merely that the operation feels quick.

stem.value: An algorithm whose running time grows quadratically takes about 1 second to process 1,000 records. Approximately how long should it be expected to take on 3,000 records?

About 3 seconds
About 9 seconds
About 1,000 seconds

explanation.value: For quadratic growth, multiplying the input size by a factor k multiplies the running time by k squared. Here the input triples, so the time increases by a factor of 3 squared, which is 9, giving about 9 seconds. The answer 3 seconds is the tempting mistake: that would be the prediction if the growth were linear rather than quadratic.

Leave the text box as is and show a red error message after the form is submitted.
Add a paragraph of instructions at the bottom of the page explaining the required format.
Silently discard the entry and leave the field blank when the format is not recognized.

explanation.value: Error prevention means designing so the mistake cannot be made in the first place; a constrained control such as a date picker makes an invalid date impossible to enter. An error message after submission is error recovery, not prevention, instructions far from the field are easily missed, and silently discarding input destroys the user's work without explanation.

stem.value: A news site presents most of its content as photographs and charts. Which change would most improve the site for users who rely on screen readers?

content.value: Increase the resolution of every image so that details are sharper when magnified.
Add accurate text alternatives that describe the meaningful content of each image and chart.
Animate the images so they fade in as the user scrolls the page.
Place all images in a single column so the page scrolls vertically.

explanation.value: A screen reader can announce only text, so images without text alternatives simply do not exist for those users. Higher resolution helps people with some usable vision but does nothing for a screen reader, and animation and column layout do not convey the information the images carry.

stem.value: A form indicates invalid fields only by turning their borders red. Which accessibility problem does this create, and what is the best fix?

content.value: Red borders load slowly, so a different color should be chosen for performance reasons.
Users who cannot distinguish red will miss the indication, so the field should also carry a text message or icon marking the error.
There is no problem, because red is a widely understood signal for an error.
The borders should be removed entirely and the invalid fields should simply be disabled.

explanation.value: Color should never be the only means of conveying information, because users with color vision deficiencies, users on monochrome displays, and screen reader users will not perceive it. Pairing the color with text or an icon makes the message available to everyone. Disabling the field would prevent the user from correcting the error at all.

stem.value: A team wants to find out whether the checkout process in its new app is easy to use before release. Which approach gives the most reliable usability evidence?

content.value: Observe people from the intended audience as they attempt realistic checkout tasks, and record where they hesitate or fail.
Have the developers who wrote the checkout code walk through it and confirm that it works.
Ask visitors to rate the color scheme of the checkout page on a five-point scale.
Measure how many lines of code the checkout process required and compare it to the previous version.

explanation.value: Usability testing means watching representative users perform real tasks, because their hesitations and errors reveal problems the designers cannot see. Developers already know how the system is meant to work, so they cannot experience it as newcomers, and opinions about color or counts of lines of code say nothing about whether people can complete the task.

stem.value: In a note-taking app, users occasionally delete the wrong note and are upset that their work is gone. Which change best reflects the principle of user control and freedom?

content.value: Remove the delete feature so that notes can never be lost.
Require users to retype the full title of a note before every deletion.
Show a brief Undo option after a deletion so the note can be restored with one action.
Record every deletion in a log file that administrators can review on request.

explanation.value: User control and freedom means giving people a clearly marked exit from unwanted states, and an easy undo lets a mistake be reversed without ceremony. Removing deletion takes away a needed capability, retyping a title burdens every correct deletion to guard against a rare mistake, and an administrator's log does not give the user their note back.

stem.value: An internal ordering system requires employees to type a four-digit department code from memory into a blank field. Replacing that field with a dropdown list of department names best illustrates which principle?

content.value: Aesthetic and minimalist design: interfaces should contain as few controls as possible.
Flexibility and efficiency: expert users should be given shortcuts.
Help and documentation: reference material should be searchable.
Recognition rather than recall: options should be visible so users do not have to remember information.

explanation.value: Recognizing a name in a visible list places far less demand on memory than recalling an arbitrary code, and it also eliminates typing errors. A dropdown does not reduce the number of controls or add a shortcut for experts, and the reference information is being built into the control rather than moved into documentation.

stem.value: When a password does not meet the site's requirements, the site displays only the message Error 422. Which revision best follows accepted guidance for error messages?

content.value: Your password must be at least 12 characters and include one number. Please add a number.
Invalid input. Please try again.
Exception thrown at PasswordValidator line 88: constraint violation.
That password is not acceptable. Contact the system administrator.

explanation.value: A good error message uses plain language, states precisely what is wrong, and tells the user how to fix it. A generic 'invalid input' does not say what to change, a raw exception exposes implementation detail the user cannot act on, and directing the user to an administrator escalates a problem they could solve themselves.

stem.value: A web application can be operated only with a mouse: several menus open on hover and cannot be reached by pressing Tab. Which change would most improve accessibility for users who cannot use a mouse?

content.value: Increase the size of the mouse pointer so the menus are easier to target.
Shorten the delay before a hover menu opens.
Add a printed manual that describes what each menu contains.
Make every interactive control reachable and operable from the keyboard, with a clearly visible focus indicator.

explanation.value: Users with motor impairments, and users of screen readers and switch devices, navigate by keyboard, so any control that cannot receive keyboard focus is unusable to them; a visible focus indicator is what tells them where they are. Pointer size and hover timing still assume a mouse, and documentation does not make the control operable.

stem.value: A page sets its body text in light gray on a white background at a fixed size of 9 pixels, and the size does not change when the user increases the browser's text size. Which statement best describes the accessibility problem?

content.value: Gray text takes longer to render than black text, slowing the page down.
Low contrast combined with small, non-resizable text makes the content hard or impossible to read for users with reduced vision.
Fixed pixel sizes prevent screen readers from announcing the text.
There is no problem, since users can zoom the entire page as an alternative.

explanation.value: Adequate contrast between text and background and the ability to enlarge text are basic accessibility requirements; failing both compounds the difficulty for users with low vision. Text color does not affect rendering speed, screen readers are unaffected by font size, and full-page zoom is a workaround that often introduces horizontal scrolling rather than a substitute for readable text.

Array indexing starts at 0, so scores[0] is 12, scores[1] is 7, and scores[2] is 25. Answering 7 comes from treating the array as though the first element were at index 1, which is the most common indexing mistake.

content.value: 18 is printed, because index 5 refers to the fifth and last element.
0 is printed, because indices past the end of an array hold the value 0.
The program fails, because the valid indices are 0 through 4 and 5 is out of bounds.
12 is printed, because the index wraps around to the beginning of the array.

explanation.value: An array of five elements has indices 0 through 4, so index 5 is past the end and the access is invalid. Off-by-one thinking produces the answer 18, but that element is at index 4. Array indices do not wrap around and reading past the end is not defined to yield 0.

The assignment stores 9 + 1, or 10, into a[1], replacing the 9. The array is then {4, 10, 1}, and the printed sum is 4 + 10 + 1, which is 15. Answering 14 uses the original contents of the array and ignores the assignment.

content.value: 2 and then 6, because the two assignments correctly exchange the values.
6 and then 6, because the second assignment restores the original value.
6 and then 2, because assignments to array elements have no effect.
2 and then 2, because the original a[0] was overwritten before it could be copied; a temporary variable is needed.

explanation.value: After the first assignment a[0] holds 2 and the original 6 is lost. The second assignment then copies that same 2 back into a[1], so both elements end up 2. A correct swap saves one value first, for example temp <- a[0], then a[0] <- a[1], then a[1] <- temp.

The first index selects the row and the second selects the column, both counted from 0. Row 1 is {5, 2, 9}, and its element at index 2 is 9. Answering 4 comes from reversing the indices and reading grid[2][1].

stem.value: A library program must store, for each book, a title (text), an author (text), a year of publication (whole number), and whether it is currently checked out (true or false). Which representation of a single book is most appropriate?

content.value: An int array of length four, with the title and author converted to numbers.
One String containing all four values joined together with commas.
Four unrelated variables per book, named book1title, book1author, and so on.
A record or object with four named fields, each declared with the type that fits the data it holds.
