explanation.value: A record groups related values of different types under meaningful field names, keeps them together as a unit, and lets each field keep its natural type. An int array cannot hold text sensibly, packing everything into one String forces the program to parse it back apart on every use, and separate numbered variables do not scale past a handful of books.

stem.value: A club roster is stored as three separate arrays, names, ages, and emails, where position i in each array refers to the same member. What is the principal risk of this design?

content.value: Arrays cannot store text, so names and emails will be lost when the program runs.
Any operation that changes one array without making the identical change to the others silently destroys the correspondence between the arrays.
Three arrays always require three times as much memory as one array of records holding the same data.
Positions in different arrays cannot be accessed with the same index value.

explanation.value: Parallel arrays rely on an unenforced convention that the same index means the same person; inserting, deleting, or sorting one array alone breaks that convention and there is no error to warn you. Storing one array of records makes each member's fields inseparable. Arrays can hold text, the total data stored is essentially the same either way, and the same index can of course be used in each array.

stem.value: A String holds the value "computer". Using zero-based indexing of its characters, which index holds the character 'p'?

explanation.value: Counting from 0: c is 0, o is 1, m is 2, and p is 3. Answering 4 counts from 1 instead of 0. The value 8 is the number of characters in the string, and the last valid index is 7.

content.value: Nothing is printed, because a void procedure cannot modify its argument.

explanation.value: Because the array is passed by reference, arr and nums name the same array in memory, so doubling element 0 inside the procedure is visible to the caller and 10 is printed. This is the important contrast with a simple int parameter, where the procedure would receive a copy and the caller's variable would be unchanged.

stem.value: A program must read and total the daily rainfall for each of 365 days, and later report the reading for any day the user names. Which is the strongest reason to store the readings in an array rather than in 365 individual variables?

content.value: An array can store values that individual variables are not capable of storing.
An array lets the program select a reading with a computed index and process all readings with a single loop, so the code does not grow with the number of days.
An array guarantees that the readings are always kept in sorted order.
An array prevents the user from ever entering an invalid rainfall value.

explanation.value: The decisive advantage is indexing: a single name plus a computed position allows one loop to handle every element and allows a day chosen at run time to be looked up directly. Separate variables would require 365 named identifiers and repeated code. Arrays do not sort themselves, do not validate input, and hold the same kinds of values a single variable can hold.

stem.value: A student recording a school choir changes the sampling rate on the recording software from 22,050 samples per second to 44,100 samples per second. What does the sampling rate control?

content.value: How loudly the recording will play back through speakers
How many distinct amplitude values each individual measurement can represent
How many times each second the amplitude of the sound wave is measured
Which compression algorithm is applied to the finished file

explanation.value: Sampling rate is the number of measurements taken per second along the continuous sound wave, so a higher rate captures more detail about how the wave changes over time. The tempting wrong answer describes bit depth, which governs the precision of each individual sample rather than how often samples are taken.

stem.value: An audio engineer re-records a track using 16 bits per sample instead of 8 bits per sample, keeping the sampling rate and the length of the recording the same. What is the primary effect of this change?

content.value: Each sample can represent a much finer set of amplitude values
Many more samples are taken during each second of the recording
The recording will play back for a longer period of time
The recording is automatically converted to a lossless file format

explanation.value: Bit depth determines how many distinct levels are available to encode each sample, so 16 bits offers far more levels than 8 bits. That finer scale reduces the rounding (quantization) error in every measurement, letting the stored values sit closer to the true shape of the wave. Bit depth does not change how frequently samples are taken; that is the sampling rate. It also has no effect on how long the recording plays or on which file format is used.

stem.value: Why is a digital recording of a real-world sound or image always an approximation of the original rather than an exact reproduction of it?

content.value: Computers can only store characters and text, so all other data must be described in words
Every digital file is required to be compressed before it can be stored
Binary numbering cannot represent values larger than 255
A continuous quantity is captured only at discrete moments and stored with a finite number of bits

explanation.value: Real-world signals vary continuously, but digitization records them only at separated instants and rounds each measurement to one of a limited set of storable values. Whatever happens between two sampling moments is never captured, and any true value falling between two representable levels is rounded away, so some detail is unavoidably lost and the result is an approximation. The other choices describe limitations that computers do not actually have: they represent all kinds of data as binary numbers of whatever width is needed, and compression is optional rather than required.

stem.value: Which statement best describes what makes a compression technique lossless?

content.value: It always produces a smaller file than any lossy technique would
The original data can be reconstructed exactly from the compressed version
It discards details that human eyes or ears are unlikely to notice
It can be applied only to images and never to text or program files

explanation.value: Lossless compression stores the data more efficiently but keeps all of it, so decompression restores the original bit for bit. Discarding imperceptible detail is the defining behavior of lossy compression, and lossless files are typically larger than lossy ones, not smaller.

stem.value: A county records office is compressing thousands of scanned contracts for long-term storage. Policy requires that any archived contract be reproducible exactly as it was scanned, because the file may later be used as evidence. Which approach best fits this requirement?

content.value: Lossy compression, because it produces the largest reduction in file size
Either type, because modern lossy methods restore the original data exactly
Lossless compression, accepting that the space savings will usually be smaller
No compression of any kind, because scanned images cannot be compressed

explanation.value: Only lossless compression guarantees that the decompressed file matches the original exactly, which is what an evidentiary archive requires. Lossy methods permanently discard data to achieve their larger savings, and they never restore the original exactly.

stem.value: In an uncompressed bitmap image, each pixel is stored using a fixed number of bits. If a graphics program changes an image from 8 bits per pixel to 24 bits per pixel, what does this primarily allow?

content.value: The image to contain three times as many pixels
The image to be displayed on a physically larger monitor
Each pixel to be one of a far larger set of distinct colors
The image to be stored without needing any file format at all

explanation.value: Bits per pixel determines how many different color values a single pixel can encode, so 24 bits allows millions of colors where 8 bits allows only 256. The number of pixels is set by the image's resolution, which is a separate property from color depth.

stem.value: Two colleagues in different cities want to exchange confidential files using symmetric encryption only. What is the central practical difficulty they face?

content.value: The same secret key must somehow reach both parties over a secure channel first
Symmetric algorithms cannot operate on files that contain non-text data
Symmetric encryption is dramatically slower than public-key encryption for large files
Symmetric ciphertext is always many times larger than the original file

explanation.value: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key for both encrypting and decrypting, so the two colleagues must get that identical key to each other over some channel an eavesdropper cannot read. Distributing the key securely is itself as hard as the problem the encryption is meant to solve, which is why this is known as the key-distribution problem. Symmetric ciphers are in fact fast, work on any binary data, and do not appreciably expand the file, so the other options misstate their behavior.

stem.value: Amara wants to send a message that only Ben will be able to read, using public-key (asymmetric) encryption. Which key should Amara use to encrypt the message?

content.value: Amara's own private key
Amara's own public key
Ben's private key
Ben's public key

explanation.value: In a public-key system, a message encrypted with a recipient's public key can be decrypted only with the matching private key, which only Ben holds. Encrypting with Amara's private key would not provide confidentiality, since anyone with her freely available public key could undo it.

stem.value: What is the essential difference between a cryptographic hash function and an encryption algorithm?

content.value: A hash function requires a secret key, while encryption requires none
A hash function is not meant to be reversed, while encryption is reversible with the correct key
A hash function can be applied only to images, while encryption applies only to text
Encryption always produces output shorter than its input, while hashing always produces longer output

explanation.value: Encryption is a two-way transformation: ciphertext exists precisely so that someone holding the correct key can recover the plaintext. Hashing is deliberately one-way, and it produces a fixed-size digest no matter how large the input is, which is why it is used to verify data rather than to recover it. Neither operation is restricted to a particular kind of file, and a hash function needs no secret key at all.

stem.value: A software publisher distributes an update along with a digital signature created using the publisher's private key. A user's system verifies that signature with the publisher's public key and it checks out. What has the user primarily gained?

content.value: Confidence that the update genuinely came from that publisher and was not altered afterward
Assurance that the contents of the update file were hidden from anyone who downloaded it
A guarantee that the update's code contains no programming errors or bugs
A faster installation process for the update on the user's system

explanation.value: A digital signature provides authenticity and integrity: only the holder of the private key could have produced a signature that verifies with the matching public key, and any modification made to the file after signing would cause verification to fail. It does not provide confidentiality, since the signed file itself remains readable by anyone who obtains it, it says nothing about the quality or correctness of the code, and it has no effect on installation speed.

stem.value: A website stores a hash of each user's password rather than the password itself. What is the strongest reason for designing the system this way?

content.value: Hashes occupy less storage space than the passwords they represent
Hashing lets support staff recover a forgotten password and email it back to the user
A stolen copy of the stored data would not hand the attacker usable passwords
Hashing the password encrypts the network connection between the browser and the server

explanation.value: Because a cryptographic hash is one-way, the stored digests cannot practically be reversed, so an attacker who steals the database does not thereby obtain the original passwords. The site can still verify a login by hashing whatever the user types and comparing it with the stored digest. The tempting distractor about emailing a forgotten password is wrong for exactly the same reason: a properly hashed password cannot be recovered by the site either. Hashing also does nothing to secure the network connection, and saving space is not the motivation, since a digest is a fixed size that is often longer than the password it replaces.

stem.value: In the vocabulary of encryption, what do the terms plaintext and ciphertext refer to?

content.value: Plaintext is the readable original message; ciphertext is the unreadable form produced by encryption
Plaintext refers to text files, while ciphertext refers to images, audio, and other binary files
Plaintext is what results when a decryption attempt fails; ciphertext is a successful decryption
Plaintext is the algorithm being used; ciphertext is the key that the algorithm requires

explanation.value: Plaintext is the input to encryption in its intelligible form, and ciphertext is the scrambled, unreadable output that the encryption process produces; decryption converts ciphertext back to plaintext. The terms describe the state of a message, not the type of file it is, whether a decryption attempt succeeded, or which parts of the system are the algorithm and the key.

stem.value: An online store must accept payment information from first-time shoppers who have never had any prior contact with the store and share no secret with it. Which property of public-key encryption makes this workable?

content.value: Public-key encryption operates without requiring any keys at all
The store's encryption key can be published openly for anyone to use
Public-key encryption processes large volumes of data faster than symmetric encryption
Public-key encryption also compresses the data it protects during transmission

explanation.value: Because the encrypting key is public and only the matching private key can decrypt, a first-time shopper can encrypt payment information without any secret having been arranged with the store in advance. That is precisely what makes secure commerce between strangers workable. Public-key encryption does use keys, it is actually slower than symmetric encryption on bulk data, and it performs no compression.

stem.value: A clinic encrypts all of its stored patient files. Which of the following risks does encryption by itself do essentially nothing to prevent?

content.value: Someone who copies the raw files off the server being able to read patient information
A stolen staff laptop's drive being examined and its records read
An eavesdropper capturing the files as they are copied to offsite backup media and reading them
An intruder deleting the files, leaving the clinic without access to its own records

explanation.value: Encryption protects confidentiality: it keeps unauthorized parties from reading data they manage to obtain, which covers the other three situations. It does not keep data from being destroyed, so availability must be protected by other means such as backups and access controls.

stem.value: Many secure connections use public-key encryption at the start of a session to establish a shared secret key, then switch to symmetric encryption for the rest of the conversation. What is the main reason for this arrangement?

content.value: Symmetric encryption is much faster for the large volume of data exchanged during a session
A public-key algorithm can encrypt only one message before its keys stop working
Symmetric encryption needs no key at all once a session has begun
Public-key algorithms cannot process data that is not plain text

explanation.value: The combination takes the strength of each approach: public-key encryption solves the problem of agreeing on a secret without a prior arrangement, and symmetric encryption then handles the bulk traffic far more efficiently. Symmetric encryption still requires the shared key throughout the session.

stem.value: A security team replaces a cipher that uses 56-bit keys with one that uses 128-bit keys. Why does this make a brute-force attack far less practical?

content.value: Longer keys cause the ciphertext to become much smaller and harder to capture
Longer keys keep the details of the algorithm itself secret from attackers
Each additional key bit doubles the number of possible keys an attacker must try
Longer keys convert a lossy cipher into a lossless one

explanation.value: A brute-force attack works by trying candidate keys one after another, and the number of candidates doubles with every additional bit of key length. Going from 56 bits to 128 bits therefore expands the search space astronomically, far beyond what exhaustive search can cover in any practical amount of time. Key length has nothing to do with ciphertext size or with hiding the algorithm, which in well-designed systems is public anyway, and ciphers are not described as lossy or lossless.

stem.value: At a conceptual level, how is digital video represented?

content.value: As one very large still image that the player stretches over time
As a sequence of still images, called frames, shown in rapid succession
As a written description of the motion that the player reconstructs on the fly
As a continuous analog waveform that is never converted into bits

explanation.value: Video digitizes motion by sampling it in time, capturing many individual images per second and displaying them quickly enough that viewers perceive continuous movement. Each frame is itself a grid of pixels, so both the spatial and the temporal dimensions are sampled, and the frames are normally paired with a separately sampled audio track.

stem.value: When a document containing letters, digits, and punctuation is saved to disk, how are those characters actually represented?

content.value: As tiny stored pictures of each individual letter shape
As an analog waveform of a person reading the text aloud
As a single hash value that the computer reverses when the file is opened
As numeric codes defined by a character encoding standard and stored in binary

explanation.value: Text is digitized by mapping every character to a number according to an agreed encoding standard, and those numbers are then stored as bits. The letter shapes people see on screen come from fonts applied at display time rather than from images stored in the file, and hashing is one-way, so it could never be reversed to recover the text.

stem.value: Which statement best describes an advantage of storing and transmitting media digitally rather than in analog form?

content.value: A digital version always occupies less storage space than an analog version
Digital representation removes the need to sample the original signal
Repeated copies of digital data do not lose quality the way analog copies do
A digital version is a perfect, complete record of the original real-world signal

explanation.value: Since digital media is just a sequence of discrete values, a copy reproduces those exact values, which avoids the generation loss that accumulates when analog recordings are duplicated again and again. Choice d overstates the case: digitization involves sampling and rounding, so the digital version is an approximation of the original signal even though copies of that digital version are exact. Digital files are not automatically smaller than analog recordings, and sampling is the very process that produces them.

stem.value: A download page lists a hash value next to a large installer file. After downloading, a user computes the hash of the file and finds that it matches the published value. What does the match establish?

content.value: That the downloaded file is, with very high probability, identical to the file the site hashed
That the file's contents were kept confidential while traveling across the network
That the file has been scanned and is guaranteed free of malicious code
That the user's copy has now been decrypted and is safe to open

explanation.value: Comparing hashes is an integrity check: because even a one-bit change would produce a very different digest, a match shows the file was not corrupted or modified relative to the one that was hashed. It reveals nothing about confidentiality during transfer, and it cannot vouch for the file's trustworthiness if the source itself is malicious.

stem.value: A three-minute passage is recorded as uncompressed audio at 22,050 samples per second using 16 bits per sample. The engineer re-records the same three-minute passage at 44,100 samples per second, still using 16 bits per sample. Compared with the first file, the second uncompressed file will be approximately

content.value: the same size, because the passage lasts the same amount of time
twice as large, because twice as many samples are stored for the same duration
half as large, because higher sampling rates pack the data more efficiently
unpredictable in size, because it depends on how loud the passage is

explanation.value: The size of an uncompressed audio file is roughly the sampling rate times the bit depth times the duration, so doubling only the sampling rate roughly doubles the number of stored samples and therefore the file size. Loudness affects the values of the samples but not how many bits are used to store them.

stem.value: A wildfire response agency builds a computer program that represents terrain, wind speed, humidity, and vegetation density, then predicts how a fire would spread hour by hour under those conditions. Which term best describes what the agency has built?

content.value: An operating system, because it manages several inputs at once
A database, because it stores terrain and weather values
A compiler, because it translates conditions into predictions
A simulation, because it projects the system's behavior over time

explanation.value: A simulation uses a model of a real system and runs that model forward in time to show how the system would behave under given conditions, which is exactly what the fire-spread program does. Storing the input values is only one part of the program; the defining feature here is projecting behavior over time from a model, not simply holding data as a database would, translating instructions as a compiler would, or managing hardware resources as an operating system would.

stem.value: An aerospace company simulates the failure of a landing gear assembly on a computer instead of physically breaking dozens of real assemblies. Which pair of advantages most directly motivates this choice?

content.value: Guaranteed accuracy and elimination of the need for physical testing
Faster network transmission and reduced storage requirements
Lower cost and reduced risk of harm compared with destructive physical testing
Automatic legal certification and regulatory approval

explanation.value: Simulations are commonly chosen because they are cheaper and safer than destroying real hardware or endangering people. They do not guarantee accuracy and do not replace physical testing or certification, so the option claiming those benefits overstates what a simulation provides.

stem.value: A team's climate model produced predictions that turned out to be far off from the observed results. Investigation showed the model's equations were coded correctly but one input constant had been entered with the wrong units. This illustrates which general limitation of simulations?

content.value: Simulations cannot represent systems that change over time
Simulation output is only as good as its assumptions and inputs
Simulations always require more computing power than is available
Simulations can only be validated by running them a second time

explanation.value: Correct code operating on bad inputs still yields bad results: a model's predictions can be no more trustworthy than the assumptions and input values it is given, and a units error in a single constant corrupts every calculation downstream of it. The failure had nothing to do with the model's ability to handle change over time, with the computing power available, or with how many times the model was run.

stem.value: Which statement best describes the relationship between a model and the real system it represents?

content.value: A model is valid only if it is expressed as a physical object rather than as software
A model must include every detail of the real system in order to be valid
A model and the real system are interchangeable once the model has been tested once
A model is a simplified representation that omits details judged unimportant

explanation.value: Modeling is fundamentally an act of abstraction: the modeler deliberately keeps the features relevant to the question being asked and discards the rest, and the details left out are precisely the ones judged unimportant for that question. Requiring every detail would make the model as complex as reality and would defeat its purpose. A model may be physical or computational without affecting its validity, and testing it once does not make it interchangeable with the real system.

stem.value: A researcher wants to estimate how often a rare combination of events occurs in a process that involves randomness. Rather than deriving the answer mathematically, she writes a program that generates random values according to the known probabilities and repeats the process one million times, then counts the outcomes. This technique is best described as:

content.value: A binary search over the outcome space
A Monte Carlo simulation of the random process
A normalization of the data set prior to analysis
A proof by induction implemented in software

explanation.value: Generating random values according to known probabilities, repeating the process a large number of times, and tallying the outcomes to approximate how often a result occurs is the defining pattern of a Monte Carlo simulation. It yields an estimate that grows more precise with more trials rather than an exact derivation, which is why the proof-by-induction option does not apply; binary search and normalization are unrelated operations that do not estimate probabilities at all.

stem.value: Two students each run the same simulation of a chemical reaction with identical settings, but their simulation includes a random element. Their results differ slightly. What is the most appropriate response?

content.value: Conclude that one student's computer has a hardware fault
Conclude the simulation is invalid because reproducible programs must give identical output
Run the simulation many more times and compare the distributions of results rather than single runs
Average the two runs and report that value as the exact answer

explanation.value: When a model contains randomness, any single run is one sample from a distribution, so meaningful comparison requires many runs. Two runs are far too few to characterize the distribution, and slight variation is expected behavior rather than evidence of a fault.

stem.value: A school district collects student survey responses in a spreadsheet. Before analyzing them, staff remove duplicate submissions, standardize date entries that were typed in three different formats, and flag rows where an age of 250 was entered. This work is best described as:

content.value: Data cleaning, which improves the reliability of later analysis
Data encryption, which protects the responses from unauthorized access
Data compression, which reduces the storage the file requires
Data visualization, which makes patterns easier to see

explanation.value: Removing duplicates, standardizing formats, and identifying impossible values are all data-cleaning activities aimed at correcting errors and inconsistencies before analysis. None of these steps encode, shrink, or graph the data.

stem.value: A city analyst reports that months with higher ice cream sales also had higher numbers of drowning incidents, and concludes that ice cream consumption causes drownings. What is the strongest objection to this conclusion?

content.value: The two variables cannot be measured on the same scale, so they cannot be compared
Monthly data can never be used to detect a relationship between variables
A correlation between two variables may be produced by a third factor that influences both
The conclusion would be valid if the analyst had used a bar chart instead of a table

explanation.value: Correlation does not establish causation: a lurking third variable, warm weather, plausibly increases both ice cream sales and time spent swimming, which would produce the observed pattern with no causal link between the two. The objection concerns the inference itself, not the measurement scales of the variables, the use of monthly data, or the choice of chart type.

stem.value: A company posts an online poll on its own product page asking, 'How satisfied are you with our product?' It receives 4,000 responses, 92 percent of them positive, and announces that 92 percent of consumers are satisfied with the product. The most serious flaw in this claim is that:

content.value: The sample size of 4,000 is too small for any conclusion
The results were reported as a percentage rather than a count
The sample is self-selected rather than representative of all consumers
Satisfaction cannot be measured numerically under any circumstances

explanation.value: People who visit the company's own product page and then choose to answer its poll are already more favorable than consumers in general, so this self-selected sample cannot support a claim about all consumers. A large sample does not fix bias: 4,000 responses collected this way are still unrepresentative. Neither the use of percentages nor the measurability of satisfaction is the central problem here.

stem.value: In a spreadsheet of 8,000 sales records, a manager wants to see only the records from the Northwest region without permanently removing the other rows from the file. Which spreadsheet operation accomplishes this?

content.value: Sorting the rows alphabetically by region
Freezing the top row of the sheet
Merging the region cells
Filtering the rows by the region column

explanation.value: Filtering temporarily hides rows that do not meet a stated condition while leaving the underlying data intact. Sorting would group Northwest rows together but would still display every other region's records as well.

stem.value: A district keeps student information in a relational database rather than in a single large spreadsheet. Which advantage most specifically favors the relational database?

content.value: It allows related information to be stored in separate linked tables
It allows numbers to be added together, which spreadsheets cannot do
It removes the need to decide what data to collect
It guarantees that all stored values are factually accurate

explanation.value: Relational databases organize data into linked tables, so a fact is stored once and referenced rather than repeated across many rows, which reduces duplication and keeps related facts consistent when something changes. Spreadsheets perform arithmetic perfectly well, no storage technology decides for you what data to collect, and none can guarantee that the values someone enters are factually accurate.

stem.value: A transit authority wants to test whether adding a fourth platform at a busy station would shorten passenger wait times before committing to construction. Compared with building the platform and observing the outcome, the main advantage of first building a computer simulation is that it:

content.value: Produces results that are certain to match what the real station will do
Eliminates the need to collect any data about current passenger behavior
Lets the authority compare many design alternatives quickly and cheaply
Replaces the need for engineers to review the design

explanation.value: Simulation lets decision makers explore alternatives that would be far too slow, costly, or permanent to test physically, so many platform configurations can be evaluated before any irreversible construction commitment is made. It still depends on real data about current passenger behavior, still yields approximations rather than certainties, and does not remove the need for engineers to review the design.

stem.value: A biologist's population model assumes unlimited food supply. When the simulation is run for 200 generations, it predicts the population growing without bound. What is the most reasonable interpretation of this result?

content.value: The result proves the biologist should run the simulation for fewer generations
The real population will grow without bound, since the simulation says so
The simulation contains a programming error, because populations cannot be modeled
The result reflects the model's unlimited-food assumption, not the real population

explanation.value: A simulation faithfully reports the consequences of its own assumptions, so unbounded growth is the expected output of an unlimited-resource assumption rather than a programming error. Because real populations are limited by food and other constraints the model deliberately leaves out, that output should not be read as a prediction about the real population; shortening the run would merely hide the behavior instead of correcting the assumption.

stem.value: A line graph of a company's monthly revenue uses a vertical axis that begins at 480 rather than at 0, and covers a range from 480 to 500. The line appears to climb steeply. What should a careful reader conclude?

content.value: Revenue grew dramatically, since the line is steep
The truncated axis exaggerates what is actually a small change
The graph is unreadable and no information can be drawn from it
Line graphs should never be used for revenue data

explanation.value: Starting the vertical axis at 480 rather than 0 spreads a 20-unit range across the full height of the chart, magnifying small differences visually, so steepness on the page does not correspond to the size of the underlying change. The graph still conveys real values; the reader simply has to read the axis rather than the slope, and line graphs remain an appropriate format for revenue over time.

stem.value: Researchers report that students who participated in an after-school tutoring program earned higher final grades than students who did not participate. Participation was voluntary. Which conclusion is best supported?

content.value: The tutoring program caused the grade difference
Participation is associated with higher grades, but not shown to cause them
The tutoring program had no effect on grades
Grades are not a valid measure of learning, so the study is meaningless

explanation.value: Because students chose whether to attend, the two groups may differ in motivation, available time, or family support, any of which could produce the grade gap independently of the tutoring. The data therefore establish an association only; a design that assigns students to groups would be needed to support a causal claim. Nothing in the results shows the program had no effect, and grades remain a usable outcome measure.

stem.value: A flight training program uses a full-motion flight simulator for a large portion of pilot instruction. Which reason for using simulation does this most clearly illustrate?

content.value: It lets trainees practice dangerous emergency scenarios safely
It proves that the aircraft design contains no defects
It removes the need for trainees to understand aircraft systems
It compresses the aircraft's flight data into a smaller file

explanation.value: Rehearsing engine failures, severe weather, and other emergencies is exactly the class of scenario that is too dangerous and too expensive to practice in a real aircraft, so a simulator lets trainees face them without risk to people or equipment. Simulators supplement a trainee's understanding of aircraft systems rather than replacing it, prove nothing about defects in the real airframe, and are not a data-compression tool.

stem.value: A researcher merges two data sets about the same 900 people: one lists a person's ID and address, the other lists a person's ID and vaccination date. Which field makes the merge possible?

content.value: The address, because it is unique to each household
The number of records, because both data sets contain 900 rows
The vaccination date, because dates are stored in a standard format
The person ID, because it identifies the same individual in both data sets

explanation.value: Combining two data sets requires a shared key that appears in both sources and uniquely identifies the same entity in each, which is exactly what the person ID provides. An address can be shared by several people in one household and a vaccination date is shared by many people, so neither reliably matches one record to one record, and equal row counts say nothing about which row corresponds to which.

stem.value: A weather service's model correctly predicted general conditions three days out but was wrong about conditions fourteen days out. Which statement best explains why long-range predictions from such models tend to be less reliable?

content.value: Computers cannot store dates more than a week in the future
The model must be rewritten in a different programming language for each forecast range
Small uncertainties in the current measurements grow as the model steps further forward in time
Long-range forecasts use fewer variables by definition

explanation.value: Each simulated time step builds on the previous one, so small errors in the initial measurements compound and the projection drifts further from reality the longer it runs. The limitation comes from error growth in the model, not from any storage or language constraint.

stem.value: Which of the following is the clearest example of using a simulation for something that could not practically be studied any other way?

content.value: Modeling the collision of two galaxies over hundreds of millions of years
Measuring the boiling point of water in a classroom laboratory
Counting the number of books in a library
Timing how long a student takes to run 100 meters

explanation.value: A galactic collision unfolds on a timescale and physical scale that no direct experiment can reproduce, so simulation is the only practical way to study it. The other three are ordinary direct measurements that are easier to perform than to model.

stem.value: An analyst has a table of 30,000 hospital visit records. She wants to know the average length of stay for each of six departments. Which sequence of conceptual data operations accomplishes this most directly?

content.value: Encrypt the records, then decrypt them one department at a time
Delete all records except the six longest stays
Sort the records by patient name, then read the first six rows
Group the records by department, then average the length-of-stay field

explanation.value: Producing a summary statistic for each category is a group-then-aggregate operation: partition the 30,000 records by department, then compute the mean of the length-of-stay field within each of the six groups. Spreadsheets and databases provide this through pivot tables or GROUP BY. Sorting by patient name or discarding records computes no per-department average and, in the deletion case, destroys the very data needed.

stem.value: A model of an ecosystem is checked by running it over a historical period for which the real outcomes are already known and comparing its output to those outcomes. This activity is best described as:

content.value: Validating the model against known real-world results
Compiling the model into machine code
Normalizing the model's data into separate tables
Encrypting the model so its assumptions remain private

explanation.value: Running a model over a historical period and comparing its output with the real outcomes already known for that period is how modelers judge whether the model represents reality well enough to be trusted, and that comparison is what validation means. The other choices name unrelated software and data operations: compiling translates code, normalizing restructures data into tables, and encrypting conceals content.

stem.value: A pie chart shows that a company's four product lines account for 40 percent, 30 percent, 20 percent, and 10 percent of this year's revenue. A reader concludes that revenue for the 40 percent product line grew compared with last year. Why is this conclusion unsupported?

content.value: Pie charts cannot represent percentages accurately
The chart shows shares of a single year's total, not change over time
The four percentages sum to 100, which indicates a data-entry error
Revenue should always be displayed as a scatter plot

explanation.value: A pie chart displays composition at one point in time, so it contains no information about any earlier year and cannot show growth or decline; the 40 percent share could accompany revenue that is higher, lower, or unchanged from last year. The four percentages summing to 100 is exactly what a correct pie chart should do, and pie charts represent proportions accurately when read for what they show.

stem.value: A team improves its traffic simulation by adding pedestrian behavior, bus schedules, and per-driver reaction times to a model that previously tracked only cars. Which trade-off should the team most expect?

content.value: The model may capture more real behavior but be harder to build and run
The model will run faster because it now has more information to work with
The model's predictions become certain once enough detail is added
Adding detail has no effect on the results a simulation produces

explanation.value: Greater fidelity generally costs more development effort, more computation, and more difficulty tracing which factor drove a particular result, so the richer traffic model becomes slower to run and harder to interpret. Added detail never converts an approximation into a certainty, and more work per time step slows execution rather than speeding it, so detail plainly does affect both the results and the cost of producing them.

stem.value: A store's data set contains a Purchase Amount column in which some rows are blank because the amount was never recorded. Which handling of these blanks is most appropriate before computing the average purchase amount?

content.value: Replace every blank with 0, since a blank means nothing was spent
Decide deliberately how to treat the missing values and report that choice
Delete the entire Purchase Amount column so the missing values cannot cause problems
Leave the blanks unexamined, because averages are unaffected by missing data

explanation.value: Missing values must be handled by an explicit, documented choice, such as excluding those rows from the calculation, because different choices produce different averages and readers need to know which one was made. Silently substituting 0 treats an unrecorded amount as a real purchase of nothing, which biases the average downward; deleting the column discards the very data being summarized; and leaving the blanks unexamined rests the average on an unstated assumption.

stem.value: A teacher explains to students that without an operating system, every application would have to include its own instructions for reading from a hard drive, drawing on the screen, and taking turns with other programs. Which idea is the teacher illustrating?

content.value: The operating system acts as a shared layer that manages hardware and resources on behalf of all applications
The operating system compiles application source code into machine code before it can run
The operating system increases the clock speed of the processor so applications run faster
The operating system stores application data permanently so that programs do not need files

explanation.value: The scenario describes duplicated work that the OS instead provides once for everyone: device access, display output, and sharing the CPU. Compilation is done by a compiler, not the OS, and the OS cannot change the processor's physical clock speed to make hardware faster.

stem.value: A student is typing a document when the power to the building suddenly fails. When the machine restarts, the last several minutes of typing are gone, even though an older version of the file is still present. Which characteristic of computer memory best explains this outcome?

content.value: Secondary storage is volatile, so its contents are erased whenever power is lost
RAM is volatile, so unsaved work held there is lost when power is lost, while saved data on storage persists
The CPU stores documents internally and clears them on every restart
Files written to storage are copied back into RAM only after a successful shutdown

explanation.value: Work in progress lives in RAM, which is volatile and loses its contents without power; the older saved version survived because it had been written to non-volatile secondary storage. Choice A reverses the two: storage is the non-volatile one.

stem.value: On a computer with a single processor core, a user has a music player, a word processor, and a file download all appearing to run at the same time. Which explanation is most accurate?

content.value: The operating system rapidly switches the core among the programs, giving each a small slice of time
The three programs are literally executing simultaneously because each has its own core
Only one program is actually running; the other two are paused until the user clicks on them
The programs are merged into a single process so the core executes one combined instruction stream written by the user

explanation.value: A single core can execute only one instruction stream at a time, so the OS scheduler interleaves the processes quickly enough that they appear concurrent. True simultaneous execution would require multiple cores or processors, which this machine does not have.

stem.value: Which statement best describes the difference between a program and a process?

content.value: A program is written in a high-level language, while a process is always written in assembly language
A program can be shared over a network, while a process must remain on one machine's hard drive
A program is a stored set of instructions, while a process is an instance of that program actually running, with its own memory and state
A program uses the CPU, while a process uses only input and output devices

explanation.value: The program is the passive file of instructions; the process is the active execution of it, tracked by the OS with allocated memory and current state. This is why opening the same text editor twice creates two processes from one program.

stem.value: During the basic instruction cycle carried out by a CPU, which sequence of steps occurs for a single instruction?

content.value: Execute the instruction, then decode it, then fetch it from memory
Fetch the instruction from memory, decode what it means, then execute it
Decode the instruction, then fetch its operands from a printer, then store it on disk
Fetch the instruction from the display, execute it, then write it back to the keyboard buffer

explanation.value: The processor must first retrieve the instruction from memory, then interpret its bit pattern to determine the operation, and only then carry it out. The other orders are impossible because an instruction cannot be decoded or executed before it has been fetched.

stem.value: A school's grade-reporting application runs on a central machine that stores all records and answers requests, while teachers use a program on their laptops to look up and update grades. This arrangement is best described as which model?

content.value: A client-server model, in which client programs send requests and a server provides the shared resource
A peer-to-peer model, in which every machine holds an equal copy of the grade records
A standalone model, in which each laptop operates without any network communication
An embedded model, in which the grade records are stored in the laptops' firmware

explanation.value: One machine holds the shared data and responds to requests, and the laptops initiate those requests, which is exactly the client-server division of roles. In peer-to-peer, no machine has that special central role and participants exchange resources directly.

stem.value: A student wants to connect a wireless headset to a phone while sitting in a park with no Wi-Fi network available. Which statement best explains why Bluetooth is the appropriate technology here?

content.value: Bluetooth requires an internet service provider, which the park supplies for free
Bluetooth is designed for short-range direct links between nearby devices and does not require a network access point
Bluetooth transmits over longer distances and at higher data rates than Wi-Fi, making it better outdoors
Bluetooth converts the phone into a wired device so no radio signal is needed

explanation.value: Bluetooth pairs two nearby devices directly over a short-range radio link, so no router, access point, or internet connection is involved. It is generally lower range and lower throughput than Wi-Fi, so the claim in choice C is backwards.

stem.value: In the context of devices communicating over a network, what is a protocol?

content.value: A physical cable standard that determines how fast electricity travels through copper
A piece of hardware installed in every computer to translate between languages
A software application that users install to browse shared files
An agreed-upon set of rules governing the format and sequence of messages exchanged between devices

explanation.value: A protocol is a shared agreement about message structure and ordering, which is what lets devices made by different manufacturers interoperate. It is a specification rather than a specific cable, chip, or application, even though hardware and software must implement it.

stem.value: What is the primary purpose of an IP address?

content.value: To identify a device on a network so that data can be delivered to the correct destination
To record the physical street location of the person operating the device
To store the device's password so that it can log in to services automatically
To measure how much bandwidth a device is permitted to use each month

explanation.value: An IP address serves as a network-level identifier that lets data be addressed and routed to a particular device. It is an addressing mechanism, not a credential, a bandwidth quota, or a precise physical address of a person.

stem.value: A computer has 16 gigabytes of RAM and a 1 terabyte solid-state drive. A student asks why the machine does not simply use the much larger drive for everything the processor is working on. Which response is most accurate?

content.value: The drive cannot hold data that changes, so only fixed values can be stored there
The processor can read and write RAM far more quickly than the drive, so active data is kept in RAM for speed
The drive is connected to the monitor rather than to the processor, so the CPU cannot reach it
RAM is cheaper per gigabyte than drive storage, so using RAM lowers the cost of the computer

explanation.value: The memory hierarchy trades capacity against speed: RAM is much faster to access than secondary storage, so the OS keeps running programs and active data there. RAM is in fact more expensive per gigabyte, which is exactly why the machine has far less of it.

stem.value: A user plugs a newly purchased scanner into a computer and the operating system reports that it must install additional software before the scanner can be used. That software is best described as which of the following?

content.value: A compiler, which translates the scanner's images into source code
A device driver, which lets the operating system communicate with that specific piece of hardware
A file system, which organizes the scanner's internal directory structure
A scheduler, which decides when the scanner is allowed to use the processor

explanation.value: A driver supplies the model-specific instructions the OS needs to control a device and interpret its signals, which is why new hardware often requires one. A scheduler manages CPU time among processes and does not teach the OS how a particular scanner works.

stem.value: Which of the following is the best description of what a file system provides?

content.value: A method of naming, organizing, and locating data stored on a device, including directories and metadata such as size and modification time
A guarantee that any file placed on the device can never be modified or deleted
A translation layer that converts documents between application formats such as text and spreadsheet
A region of the processor that holds the results of arithmetic operations

explanation.value: A file system imposes structure on raw storage so that named files can be created, found, and described by metadata. It does not convert between application document formats, which is the job of the applications themselves.

stem.value: A computer lab administrator must run the same setup steps on 40 machines and wants to save the steps in a script that can be repeated exactly. Which comparison of user interfaces best supports choosing a command-line interface over a graphical one for this task?

content.value: A command-line interface is the only interface that can access files stored on a hard drive
A graphical interface runs without an operating system, so it cannot be used for administration
Commands are text instructions that can be recorded and replayed, making repeated tasks easy to automate
Commands execute directly in hardware without being processed by the operating system, so they are always faster

explanation.value: Because command-line actions are expressed as text, they can be stored in a script and run identically on many machines, which is the key advantage here. Both interfaces run on top of the OS and both can reach the same files; the difference is automatability, not capability or bypassing the OS.

stem.value: Several programs are open at once and together they request more memory than the machine physically has installed. The system keeps running by moving portions of memory that are not currently being used out to the drive and bringing them back when needed. This technique is known as which of the following?

content.value: Caching frequently used instructions inside the processor
Compiling programs into a smaller machine-code representation
Defragmenting the drive to place file blocks in contiguous order
Virtual memory, in which storage space is used to extend the apparent amount of main memory

explanation.value: Virtual memory lets the OS present more addressable memory than is physically installed by swapping inactive portions to disk. Caching moves data in the opposite direction, toward faster storage close to the CPU, rather than extending capacity.

stem.value: Which of the following lists contains only input devices?

content.value: Microphone, mouse, barcode scanner
Keyboard, speaker, webcam
Monitor, printer, projector
Touchscreen, trackpad, headphones

explanation.value: A microphone, a mouse, and a barcode scanner all send data into the computer and produce no output from it. The other lists each include at least one output device, and a touchscreen is properly a combined input and output device.

stem.value: A student claims that buying a processor with twice the clock speed will always make every program on the computer finish in half the time. Which response best corrects this claim?

content.value: The claim is correct, because clock speed determines total running time by itself
The claim is wrong because clock speed has no effect at all on how fast a program runs
The claim overlooks other factors, such as waiting on storage, memory, or a network, that can limit a program's speed regardless of processor speed
The claim is wrong because a faster processor can execute only one program at a time, while a slower one can execute many

explanation.value: Programs that spend much of their time waiting on input/output or memory are limited by those components, so doubling clock speed does not halve their runtime. Clock speed does matter for compute-bound work, so the opposite extreme in choice B is also false.

stem.value: Two students on the same home network share files: one machine keeps a copy of every file and each machine can both request files from and supply files to the other, with no central machine in charge. Compared with a client-server arrangement, which statement about this peer-to-peer arrangement is accurate?

content.value: Each participant can act as both a requester and a provider, so no single dedicated machine must be available for sharing to work
Peer-to-peer arrangements require a dedicated always-on machine, while client-server arrangements do not
Peer-to-peer arrangements cannot use IP addresses, because addressing is a client-server feature
In peer-to-peer, only one machine may hold a copy of a given file at any time

explanation.value: The defining feature of peer-to-peer is that participants take on both roles, removing the dependence on one central server. Choice B reverses the models, and both models rely on ordinary network addressing.

stem.value: On a shared classroom computer, each student signs in with a separate account and can open only the files in their own folder. Which operating system responsibility does this illustrate?

content.value: Managing user accounts and access permissions to control who may read or modify which resources
Translating high-level source code into instructions the processor can execute
Increasing the amount of physical storage available on the drive
Choosing which network cable the computer should use to reach the internet

explanation.value: Maintaining accounts and enforcing permissions on files is a core protection function of the operating system on a multi-user machine. Translation of source code is done by compilers or interpreters, which are separate tools that happen to run on the OS.

stem.value: Inside a computer, the processor, main memory, and input/output controllers are connected by a shared set of electrical pathways. What is the main function of these pathways, collectively called a bus?

content.value: To perform arithmetic and logic operations on data before it reaches memory
To carry data, addresses, and control signals between the components of the system
To store the operating system permanently so it survives a power loss
To convert wireless radio signals into text that applications can display

explanation.value: A bus is the communication channel that moves data along with the addresses and control signals that say where it goes and what should happen to it. Arithmetic is performed in the CPU's arithmetic logic unit, not on the interconnect itself.

stem.value: A school is deciding between running network cable to each desk in a computer lab and equipping the lab with a wireless access point. Which statement describes a genuine trade-off between the two approaches?

content.value: Wired connections generally offer more consistent speed and less interference, while wireless offers greater mobility and lower installation effort
Wireless connections can carry data, while wired connections can carry only electrical power
Wired connections work only for computers, while wireless connections work only for phones
Wireless connections never require any device to be plugged into anything, including the access point itself

explanation.value: The real trade-off is reliability and throughput versus flexibility and cost of installation, which is what choice A captures. Choice D is wrong because the access point itself is normally wired to the network and to power.

stem.value: When a computer is first powered on, instructions stored in non-volatile memory on the motherboard run first, check the hardware, and then load the operating system from storage into RAM. This overall process is best described as which of the following?

content.value: Compiling, in which the operating system's source code is translated each time the machine starts
Booting, in which built-in startup firmware initializes hardware and loads the operating system into memory
Scheduling, in which the processor decides the order in which user applications will run
Formatting, in which the drive is prepared with a new file system before the operating system can start

explanation.value: The startup sequence run by firmware that checks hardware and hands control to the operating system is called booting. The OS is loaded as already-compiled machine code, so no compilation happens at startup, and formatting erases and prepares a drive rather than starting the machine.

stem.value: A community theater company has computers in its box office, lighting booth, and costume shop, all located inside one building and connected by cabling the company owns. The company also connects to a rehearsal studio twelve miles away using circuits leased from a telecommunications provider. Which description best classifies these two networks?

content.value: Both networks are LANs, because both carry the theater company's own traffic.
The in-building network is a LAN, and the link to the distant studio makes the combined network a WAN.
The in-building network is a WAN, and the link to the distant studio is a LAN.
Neither is a LAN or a WAN, because leased circuits are used.

explanation.value: A LAN spans a small, single-site geographic area with infrastructure the owner controls, which describes the in-building network. Once the network spans a long distance over links leased from a carrier, it is a WAN. Ownership of traffic is irrelevant to the classification; geographic span and the kind of infrastructure used are what distinguish the two.

stem.value: When a large file is transmitted across the Internet, it is divided into packets rather than sent as one continuous stream. Which statement best explains the primary advantage of this design?

content.value: Packets are automatically compressed, so the total number of bits sent is reduced.
Packets are encrypted by default, so the contents cannot be read in transit.
Packets can travel independently over different available paths and only a lost packet must be resent, rather than the whole file.
Packets guarantee that data arrives at the destination in exactly the order it was sent.

explanation.value: Packet switching lets routers forward each packet along whatever path is currently available, so links can be shared efficiently and a single failure only requires retransmitting one small packet. Ordering is not guaranteed by packet switching itself; a higher-layer protocol such as TCP reassembles packets into the correct order, and packetization provides neither compression nor encryption.

stem.value: A school's satellite Internet link can transfer 200 megabits per second, but every request takes about 600 milliseconds to receive its first response. Students report that downloading a large video file finishes quickly, while an interactive coding terminal feels sluggish. Which statement best accounts for this?

content.value: The link has high bandwidth but also high latency; bulk transfers benefit from bandwidth while interactive work is dominated by round-trip delay.
The link has low bandwidth but low latency; interactive work needs more total throughput than a video download.
Bandwidth and latency are the same measurement, so the reported numbers must be in error.
Latency affects only uploads, so downloads of any kind are unaffected by it.

explanation.value: Bandwidth is how much data can move per unit of time, while latency is the delay before data begins arriving. A large download is bandwidth-bound and can stream at full rate once started, but an interactive session sends many small messages, each paying the round-trip delay, so high latency makes it feel slow even when bandwidth is ample.

stem.value: In a network arranged as a star topology, every device connects to one central switch. Which of the following is the most significant disadvantage of this arrangement?

content.value: A break in any single device's cable disconnects all other devices as well.
Failure of the central device disconnects every device on the network.
Devices cannot be added or removed once the network is in operation.
Each device must be assigned the same network address as the central device.

explanation.value: A star topology concentrates all traffic through one central node, making that node a single point of failure. Its compensating strength is that one damaged cable isolates only the device on that cable and that adding or removing devices is easy, which is why the other options are incorrect.

stem.value: A regional emergency-services agency needs a network in which the loss of any single link still leaves every site able to reach every other site. Which topology best meets this requirement?

content.value: A bus topology, in which all sites share one common backbone cable.
A star topology centered on the agency's headquarters.
A mesh topology, in which sites have multiple direct connections to one another.
A single ring topology connecting the sites in one loop.

explanation.value: A mesh topology provides redundant paths, so traffic can be rerouted when a link fails. A bus fails entirely if the backbone breaks, a star fails if the center fails, and a simple one-directional ring is broken by a single cut, so none of those guarantees continued full connectivity.

stem.value: Which statement most accurately describes the difference in role between a switch and a router in a typical school network?

content.value: A switch forwards traffic among devices within the same local network, while a router forwards traffic between different networks.
A switch encrypts traffic leaving the building, while a router decrypts traffic entering it.
A switch stores web pages locally, while a router requests them from the Internet.
A switch assigns domain names to devices, while a router converts those names to numeric addresses.

explanation.value: Switches operate within a single local network, delivering frames to the correct local device, while routers examine destination network addresses and forward packets between separate networks. Encryption, caching of pages, and name resolution are handled by other services entirely, not by the basic forwarding roles of these two devices.

stem.value: A student notices that a laptop has both a MAC address and an IP address. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?

content.value: The MAC address is a hardware identifier fixed to the network interface, while the IP address is a logical address that can change when the laptop joins a different network.
The MAC address changes each time the laptop connects to a network, while the IP address is permanently burned into the hardware.
Both addresses are assigned by the same server and always change together.
The MAC address is used to route packets across the Internet, while the IP address is used only inside the building.

explanation.value: A MAC address identifies the physical network interface and is used for delivery within a local network segment, while an IP address is a logical address tied to the network the device is currently on and typically changes when the device moves. Internet routing is done using IP addresses, not MAC addresses, which is why the last option reverses the true roles.

stem.value: A user types a website's name into a browser and the page loads. What role does the Domain Name System play in this process?

content.value: It compresses the requested page so it transfers more quickly.
It translates the human-readable domain name into a numeric IP address the browser can connect to.
It stores a copy of the website's HTML so the origin server does not have to respond.
It verifies the user's password before allowing the connection to proceed.

explanation.value: DNS is a distributed lookup service that maps names such as example.org to the IP addresses needed to open a connection. It does not host or cache page content, compress data, or perform user authentication; those are functions of web servers, content delivery networks, and identity systems.

stem.value: Consider the URL https://library.example.edu/catalog/search?subject=biology. Which part of this URL identifies the host that the browser will contact?

content.value: https
library.example.edu
/catalog/search
subject=biology

explanation.value: The portion between the scheme's double slashes and the next slash is the host (domain) name, which DNS resolves to the server's address. The leading https is the scheme or protocol, /catalog/search is the path to a resource on that server, and subject=biology is a query-string parameter passed to the resource.

stem.value: HTTP is described as a stateless protocol. Which consequence follows most directly from statelessness, and how do websites commonly work around it?

content.value: The server cannot send images, so pages embed image data directly in the HTML.
The server retains no memory of previous requests, so sites store a cookie in the browser that is sent back with later requests to identify the session.
The server cannot handle more than one client at a time, so sites use load balancers to queue requests.
The server cannot use encryption, so sites add a separate password prompt on every page.

explanation.value: Statelessness means each HTTP request is handled independently, with nothing in the protocol itself linking it to earlier requests from the same client. Cookies solve this by storing a small identifier in the browser that is returned with subsequent requests, letting the server associate them with a session; concurrency, images, and encryption are unrelated to statelessness.

stem.value: A student submits a form on a page served over HTTPS while using a coffee shop's shared wireless network. Which protection does HTTPS provide in this situation?

content.value: It prevents the website's own operators from reading the submitted data.
It guarantees that the website is trustworthy and will handle the data responsibly.
It encrypts the data in transit so someone monitoring the wireless network cannot read the form contents.
It scans the submitted data for malware before the server receives it.

explanation.value: HTTPS wraps HTTP in TLS, which encrypts traffic between the browser and the server and protects it from eavesdroppers on the network path. It says nothing about the site's honesty or internal data handling, since the server necessarily decrypts and reads what the user sends, and it performs no malware scanning.

stem.value: During a TLS connection, a browser receives a digital certificate from the server. What is the primary purpose of that certificate?

content.value: To let the browser verify, through a trusted certificate authority, that the server's public key genuinely belongs to the named domain.
To supply the browser with the shared secret key that will encrypt the rest of the session.
To store the user's login credentials so they do not need to be typed again.
To compress the server's responses so the page loads faster.

explanation.value: A certificate binds a public key to a domain name and is signed by a certificate authority the browser already trusts, which is what lets the client authenticate the server and resist impersonation. The session key is not shipped inside the certificate; it is negotiated during the handshake using that verified public key material.

stem.value: Which statement correctly contrasts symmetric-key encryption with public-key (asymmetric) encryption?

content.value: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key for both encrypting and decrypting, while public-key encryption uses a mathematically related key pair in which one key encrypts and the other decrypts.
Symmetric encryption requires two different keys, while public-key encryption requires only one key known to both parties.
Symmetric encryption can only be used on text, while public-key encryption can be used on any file type.
Symmetric encryption is irreversible, while public-key encryption can be reversed by the sender.

explanation.value: Symmetric schemes use a single secret key that both parties must already share, which makes key distribution the hard problem. Public-key schemes use a key pair, so a freely published public key can be used to encrypt a message that only the matching private key can decrypt; neither scheme is irreversible, which distinguishes encryption from hashing.

stem.value: A researcher wants a colleague to be able to send her a confidential file that only she can read, without the two of them meeting first to exchange a secret. Using public-key cryptography, what should happen?

content.value: The colleague encrypts the file with the researcher's public key, and the researcher decrypts it with her private key.
The colleague encrypts the file with the researcher's private key, and the researcher decrypts it with her public key.
The colleague encrypts the file with his own private key, and the researcher decrypts it with that same private key.
The researcher publishes her private key so the colleague can encrypt the file with it.

explanation.value: For confidentiality, the sender encrypts with the recipient's freely published public key, so only the holder of the matching private key can decrypt. Encrypting with a private key is used for digital signatures rather than secrecy, since anyone holding the corresponding public key could undo it, and a private key must never be published.

stem.value: A district installs a firewall at the boundary between its internal network and the Internet. Which description best characterizes what a firewall does?

content.value: It inspects network traffic and permits or blocks it according to a configured set of rules.
It encrypts all traffic leaving the district so that outside observers cannot read it.
It creates redundant copies of district data at an offsite location.
It removes viruses from files already stored on district computers.

explanation.value: A firewall is a traffic filter that decides which connections may pass based on rules about addresses, ports, protocols, or application behavior. Encrypting outbound traffic is the job of a VPN or TLS, offsite copies are backup, and cleaning infected files is antivirus software; conflating these functions is the most common error on this topic.

stem.value: A teacher working from a hotel needs to reach a grading system that is only reachable from inside the school's private network. The school tells her to connect to its VPN first. What does the VPN accomplish?

content.value: It scans her laptop for malware before allowing the grading system to load.
It creates an encrypted tunnel over the public Internet so her laptop can communicate as though it were attached to the school's private network.
It increases the hotel network's bandwidth so the grading system responds faster.
It replaces the school's firewall so that all internal systems become publicly reachable.

explanation.value: A VPN encapsulates and encrypts traffic between a remote device and a private network, effectively extending that network across untrusted infrastructure. It adds encryption and overhead rather than bandwidth, and it works alongside a firewall rather than exposing internal systems to the public.

stem.value: A network administrator finds that a single infected machine on the network spread malicious code to dozens of other machines on its own, with no user on those machines opening a file or clicking anything. Which category of malware best fits this behavior?

content.value: A worm, which self-replicates and spreads across a network without requiring user action.
A Trojan horse, which spreads by disguising itself as a program the user chooses to install.
Spyware, which silently records user activity and reports it to a third party.
Ransomware, which encrypts a victim's files and demands payment for the key.

explanation.value: The defining property of a worm is autonomous self-propagation, typically by exploiting network-reachable vulnerabilities, so no user interaction is needed on the victim machines. A Trojan depends on a user being tricked into running it, and spyware and ransomware are defined by their payload rather than by how they spread.

stem.value: A web application builds a database query by pasting whatever text a visitor types into a search box directly into the query string. An attacker enters text crafted so that part of it is interpreted as query syntax rather than as search text. Which countermeasure most directly prevents this class of attack?

content.value: Serving the page over HTTPS instead of HTTP.
Using parameterized queries so that user input is always treated as data rather than as executable query syntax.
Requiring visitors to create an account before searching.
Increasing the server's available memory and processing power.

explanation.value: This is an injection attack, and it is caused by mixing untrusted input with code, so the fix is to separate them using parameterized queries (with input validation as an additional layer). HTTPS protects data in transit but delivers the malicious input just as faithfully, and authentication or more hardware does nothing to stop an authenticated or patient attacker.

stem.value: On an unsecured public wireless network, an attacker positions equipment so that a victim's traffic passes through the attacker's device, which relays it to the intended destination while reading and altering it. Which attack is described, and which measure most directly defends against it?

content.value: A brute-force attack, defended against by choosing a longer password.
A man-in-the-middle attack, defended against by using end-to-end encrypted connections whose server certificates the client verifies.
A buffer-overflow attack, defended against by adding more memory to the victim's device.
A ransomware attack, defended against by keeping offline backups of important files.

explanation.value: Interposing on a communication path to read or modify traffic in transit is a man-in-the-middle attack. Verified TLS connections defeat it because the attacker cannot produce a valid certificate for the destination domain and cannot read the encrypted contents; password length, memory size, and backups address entirely different threats.

stem.value: Which of the following best describes the technical mechanism by which a phishing message compromises an account?

content.value: It exploits a flaw in the mail server's software to read stored messages directly.
It floods the login server with traffic until the server accepts any credentials.
It presents a counterfeit page or request that impersonates a trusted party, causing the user to hand over credentials that the attacker then replays against the real service.
It breaks the encryption protecting the user's stored password file.
